subtopic: SEARCH AND RESCUE
subsubtopic: SINKING OF "ARCTIC EXPLORER" OFF NEWFOUNDLAND- MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity. Some time on the morning of July 3 the Canadian motor vessel Arctic Explorer sank off the northern tip of Newfoundland with the loss of 13 lives. From the time the vessel was reported missing it took over five hours to get search aircraft in the area. This could have been a critical factor. The commanding officer of the search and rescue co-ordinating centre in Halifax said in an interview last December 26:
The Canadian armed forces rescue co-ordination centre here is so short of manpower and aircraft it could not respond to a mid-ocean tragedy.
He went on to say:
-we need fixed wing support out of Gander, Newfoundland.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay):
That this House directs the Minister of National Defence to take immediate steps to have fixed wing aircraft stationed in Newfoundland in order to reduce the critical time factor in getting search operations under way off the coast of Newfoundland and in the northwest Atlantic.

subsubtopic: NEED FOR ADDITIONAL RESOURCES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43

POST OFFICE
subsubtopic: TIMING OF PARLIAMENTARY SUMMER RECESS-EFFECT ON POSTAL STRIKE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. It deals with the stand-off in the negotiations in the postal strike. On Friday the Prime Minister indicated the government's position on the strike when he said:
We have taken the clear position that there is no intention to settle this strike by legislation. It will, and should be settled by the bargaining process.

July 6. 1981
Oral Questions
In view of what appears to be the present state of the negotiations, or the lack of negotiations, and that the government House leader indicated that the House may well rise on July 10 for a recess until the Wednesday following Thanksgiving, does the Prime Minister think it is wise to adjourn the House before this particular dispute has been resolved and settled? Will he in fact allow the House to recess over the summer months before the strike is resolved?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: POST OFFICE
subsubtopic: TIMING OF PARLIAMENTARY SUMMER RECESS-EFFECT ON POSTAL STRIKE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my understanding is that our House leader has never indicated any precise date. I think the date of July 10 was mentioned by the Conservative House leader. We will adjourn as soon as the business before the House is completed in an acceptable fashion. I repeat that part of that business is not to legislate a return of the CUPW.
* (1415)
It seems to me that the union leaders have put themselves in a difficult position for us to satisfy them. Mr. Parrot has made it clear that, if legislated back to work, he would disobey the order. He seems to be making it clear by his actions that he does not want to return to the bargaining table. Therefore, I am at a loss to know what would advance negotiations or a settlement in this area. Certainly we do not want to legislate a union back for many reasons, but at this particular time when the union leader himself says that he would rather go to jail than obey the law I do not know why the hon. member would suggest legislation right now, under those circumstances.

subtopic: POST OFFICE
subsubtopic: TIMING OF PARLIAMENTARY SUMMER RECESS-EFFECT ON POSTAL STRIKE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the proposition which the Prime Minister puts forward is a rather novel one. He says that he is afraid to legislate if there is some concern that the full force of law would not be brought to bear against those who do not obey it.

subtopic: EFFECT OF STRIKE ON SMALL BUSINESS
EFFECT OF STRIKE ON SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is for the President of the Treasury Board. On June 30 the minister said:
-that members opposite have no monopoly on concern for the people of Canada and the difficulties they will have in enduring this strike.
I would like to ask the minister about his concern for the businessman, particularly the small businessmen of this country. As we all know, many businesses are staggering under the burden of the government's unprecedented interest rates. Bankruptcies are soaring. It is estimated by the Canadian Organization of Small Business that there will be between
1,000	and 1,500 bankruptcies per week as a result of the postal strike. Can the minister explain to the small business community how his concern will help them to remain solvent? I know that the minister's paycheck is delivered by messenger, but what about the rest of the people of Canada? What does he propose to do to help them?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
subtopic: EFFECT OF STRIKE ON SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I remain in contact with the small
business community. I had a discussion with Mr. Bulloch this morning in order to get a feeling of what the circumstances are. He is monitoring the problems and the costs. I hope the banks are responsive to representations being made that where it is clear that accounts are mounting because of the postal strike, per se, consideration will be given to businessmen in those circumstances.

subtopic: ROLE OF POSTMASTER GENERAL
ROLE OF POSTMASTER GENERAL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my final supplementary question is for the hidden cabinet minister in this whole business, that is, the Postmaster General, who I am sure has a passing interest in this matter. I am sure after what he did last year he has been kept out of the negotiations this year.
The Canada Post Corporation is scheduled to be brought into effect on September 1 of this year. I know that the Postmaster General will not want this new corporation to start up under the pall of having its employees on strike. Is it the minister's intention to proceed with the order in council which would bring the Crown corporation into effect on September 1 and to transfer the negotiations in this matter to the Crown corporation and away from the Treasury Board, or will he just sit by and let matters drift, allowing this strike to carry on for the duration of the summer and until Parliament reconvenes?

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: ROLE OF POSTMASTER GENERAL
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the date of September 1 is an objective we have in mind. Of course several events may occur between now and September 1 which will make it difficult to proclaim the act at that time. I simply want to remind the hon. member that nowhere is there a firm and written guarantee that the Act to establish the Canada Post Corporation will be proclaimed on September 1. It is a date we have set as an objective and the Post Office officials who are busy drafting the regulations and setting in motion the provisional mechanisms to change the department into a Crown Corporation will be ready around September 1. It is, unfortunately, too early for me to be in a position to say whether or not the proclamation will take place on that date.

subtopic: DELIVERY OF SOCIAL SECURITY CHEQUES
DELIVERY OF SOCIAL SECURITY CHEQUES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, pensions, family allowances, veterans' allowances and unemployment insurance cheques are very important elements in many families for meeting their expenses these days. I have a question for the Minister of Supply and Services in view of a response that he gave in the House on Friday. He said that at that time talks were under way with the letter carriers' union to see whether they would assist in the distribution of this type of cheque during the course of the postal strike. At that time he said that he was not sure what the status would be. I would
July 6, 1981

ask the minister now if he could provide information to the House as to what the position will be regarding the delivery of these cheques in the future.

subtopic: DELIVERY OF SOCIAL SECURITY CHEQUES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if I understood the hon. gentleman's question properly, I can tell him that the negotiations, or at least the discussions with the LCUC have not as yet been completed. They are being conducted by officials within the administration of the Post Office. I might say to the hon. gentleman that while the indications are positive that the LCUC would carry through and would deliver the cheques, I insisted that that undertaking be given to me in writing. As I indicated on Friday, in the event that we are unable to obtain such an undertaking in writing, we will have a series of distribution centres throughout the country which will be responsible for the distribution of the socioeconomic cheques that the hon. gentleman has identified.
[ Translation]
And those cheques, Madam Speaker, include, as I indicated on Friday, pension cheques, family allowances, old age security, the supplements and all pensions distributed throughout Canada, including the Canada Pension Plan benefits.
speakername: Hon.   J.-J. Blais@Minister of Supply and Services

subtopic: DELIVERY OF JUNE CHEQUES
DELIVERY OF JUNE CHEQUES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same minister. On Friday the minister did state that all the cheques which were due in the month of June had been delivered. I would point out that the information he had received is wrong. There are many of us on this side of the House who have received phone calls from individuals who expected those cheques. They have not been received.
I would first like to ask the minister what action he is proposing to ensure that those cheques are delivered. Second, in the establishment of the emergency distribution centres, would the minister take account of the problems which many individuals have in reaching these centres? As an example it is very awkward to get unemployment insurance cheques today in rural communities and in centres like Metropolitan Toronto. In Toronto the distribution centre is at Broadview and Queen. It is not convenient at all to the normal rapid transit services. In addition to that, the people who are expecting cheques do not know whether their cheques are in before they arrive down there, so they may take a long trip and find out that there are no cheques available. Would the minister ensure that there are more convenient means available to citizens to pick up these cheques when he is establishing this emergency distribution process?

I might indicate, first of all, with reference to the first part of the hon. gentleman's question, that I would appreciate it if all members of this House would advise me in the event that there are any cheques due in June which have not been received, and I will
Oral Questions
ensure that those cheques are forwarded as soon as practicable. If there are a number of them, that number has not been communicated to me.
I see that the hon. member for Yukon is identifying himself as one recipient who has not received his cheque.

speechtext: No, no!

I would be pleased to receive further particulars relating to that particular failing.
In terms of the distribution centres, I might advise the hon. gentleman that we are attempting, in all instances, to have storefront operations for areas which are readily accessible to the total population. I would appreciate any co-operation that all hon. members of the House might be able to provide me in order to ensure that those individuals who are entitled to cheques are made aware of the circumstances of the distribution. subtopic: GOVERNMENT STEPS TO RE-ESTABLISH NEGOTIATING PROCESS
GOVERNMENT STEPS TO RE-ESTABLISH NEGOTIATING PROCESS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, may I address a further question on the postal situation to the Prime Minister. In view of the Prime Minister's clear statement on Friday, and again today, that the government does not intend to bring this dispute to a conclusion by introducing back to work legislation, a position with which he knows we agree, but in view of the seriousness of the situation, and the suffering that is being endured, what positive steps is the government prepared to take to try to re-establish the process of negotiating? To what extent is the government prepared to move in the hope that the other side might also move to a certain extent, so that the two parties can be got back to the bargaining table? Since the Prime Minister says that is the way it must be done, will the government do its part in getting back to the bargaining process?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: GOVERNMENT STEPS TO RE-ESTABLISH NEGOTIATING PROCESS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as far as the first part of the question is concerned, which asks what the government is doing to try to have negotiations resume, I have a letter from the President of the Treasury Board, of which I am sure he would send a copy to the hon. member, indicating the times when we have attempted to get CUPW back to the negotiating table from which it withdrew the Friday before the strike. There were direct and indirect attempts to get them to come to the bargaining table, including, I believe, one at ten o'clock on Monday evening. The union leaders have consistently refused to come to the table.
In so far as the hon. member's suggestion is concerned, that I might indicate what we are prepared to do in order to incite them back, I would think that the hon. member is too experienced in matters of labour relations to think it would be appropriate for me to indicate any particular area where

July 6, 1981
Oral Questions
bargaining can and should take place. The process of bargaining should take place between union leaders and government representatives, not between the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, eminent as he is, and myself, as uneminent as I am.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT STEPS TO RE-ESTABLISH NEGOTIATING PROCESS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON ITEMS IN JASMIN REPORT
GOVERNMENT POSITION ON ITEMS IN JASMIN REPORT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, first may I make it clear that I used the word "encourage", not the word "incite". May I say to the Prime Minister that we are prepared to admit that there have been faults on both sides in the past. The question is what can now be done? In particular, if the government is not prepared to agree in advance to all of the conditions set out in the Jasmin report, is the government prepared to indicate which of those conditions it will accept, which of those conditions it will discuss, in the hope that this might encourage the other side at least to resume the negotiating process?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON ITEMS IN JASMIN REPORT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am absolutely certain that once the parties sit down at the bargaining table the President of the Treasury Board, through his officials and negotiators, will indicate some areas where we are prepared to reject and perhaps some we are prepared to accept. Once again that is a matter for the negotiating process, not for an informal exchange of views between the hon. member and myself.
In so far as his correction about encouragement rather than incitement is concerned, I should have thought it would be encouragement enough for the workers to know that they would be able to resume the service that the people of Canada want and desire, they would be able to see their fellow workers return to work, they would be able to see small businessmen taken out of the difficult straits that have been described in this House and, perhaps, even most important, that they would be looking forward to the prospect of some $25,000 per year payment for the average letter sorter. That does not seem like a bad enticement, Madam Speaker, to come to the table.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER SEEK ADVICE
REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER SEEK ADVICE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, again I say that we appreciate the fact that there have been faults on both sides in the past. We are not now discussing the past; we are now discussing the impasse. I have been trying to get from the Prime Minister some willingness to do something that would get the two sides together. If he does not have any ideas along this line, may I remind him that the Minister for Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the hon. member for Lincoln on previous occasions, in the midst of all night sessions, were able to settle some of these disputes. Would he seek some advice from them in the hope that we might get action soon?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER SEEK ADVICE
speechtext: I take that, Madam Speaker, apart from the fact that it rests with some members on this side, as a suggestion. I will consider the suggestion.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question was not intended to be critical of the coast guard but the search and rescue capability as it exists at the present time. But the minister will be aware that reaction time could be a critical factor, and only an inquiry will determine that. No doubt the minister is aware also that on December 26 of last year the Commanding Officer of the Canadian Armed Forces Rescue Co-Ordination Centre in Halifax said:
The Canadian Armed Forces Rescue Co-Ordination Centre here is so short of manpower and aircraft it could not respond to a mid-ocean tragedy.
He referred to the task as trying to cover an amputation with a band-aid. He went on to emphasize the desperate need for the stationing of fixed wing aircraft in Newfoundland.
There was a reaction time in this case. It took almost five hours to get the fixed wing aircraft into the search area. During that period men were in the water. This reaction time could have been cut to less than half that taken if these aircraft had been operating out of Newfoundland. The minister knows that helicopters can only effect a rescue. It takes fixed wing aircraft to effect a search.
Why did the government not respond to this recommendation of the commanding officer of the Rescue Co-Ordination Centre and I might also add the recommendation of his colleague, the Minister of National Revenue? The Minister of National Revenue expressed his concern last August over the lack of a search and rescue capability, referring to the fact that marine disaster calls had risen by 62 per cent in the area. That is a serious situation. I do not want to make capital out of it, but how many more people have to die before these people are listened to?

Be that as it may, a preliminary investigation has already been ordered by the Minister of Transport. Two investigators are already at the site and hopefully we will get to know more about the real causes of the tragedy.

subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext: The House resumed, from Friday, July 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pepin that Bill S-6, to amend the Two-Price Wheat Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when I was speaking on Friday last about this bill I was emphasizing the fact that unfortunately it has turned out to be an act of fraud on western farmers. I say that for these reasons. In 1974 the government was supposed to be putting forward a subsidy for farmers producing wheat for human consumption in Canada. This has turned out to be a subsidy for consumers and a large proportion of it was paid for by producers. The second point was that, in effect, it was a seven-year price control mechanism which no other sector of the community had to endure. The third point is that this particular bill is retroactive for nearly three years to avoid a $200 million liability.
Therefore I suggest, for those three reasons, that something should be done to this bill; either take it out and bring it in again, or postpone it for a while and change it so that we do not have this continuing act of fraud laid on our shoulders.
The final point is that in the view of western Canadians, due to the acts of this Parliament, we have had to suffer a series of hammer blows over the last 35 years: the British wheat agreement of 1946-50; the dropping of the international wheat agreement in 1968; the price cutting periods we have experienced in the last 15 years; the LIFT program which deliberately took farmers out of production of a product desperately needed by the world's hungry. More recently we have had the Russion embargo fiasco, the messed up fodder program, the messed up herd maintenance program, and over the last 15 years we have had the railways and grain companies deliberately trying to get out of the grain business. More recently again we have had this renewed fight over the Crows-nest Pass rates, the fight over the last year on energy pricing and the Constitution. These are all part of what western Canadians feel is a direct attack on them as westerners. Unfortunately, if you look at the figures, this is not for the good of Canada.
So I would like to suggest that the House recommend to the government that it drop this bill, draft a new one which proposes a genuine two-price system for farmers so that Canadian farmers, whether they be in the east or the west, who produce wheat for human consumption in Canada can get the same protection for their product as other sectors of the economy.

subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill S-6 is an attempt to legalize what the government has been doing for some time. The fact that what it has been doing has been
July 6, 1981

going on since 1978 is a pretty fair indication of the commitment and interest the government has shown in agriculture over those years. It is also a pretty fair indication of the kind of speedy action we are going to get on agricultural problems from this government. If it has taken them three years to repeal a portion of an act, we will wait a long time for more substantial legislation. Why is it that the government always requires farmers to pay for what happens? We must take a look at this particular bill and at the whole range of agricultural legislation.
During the war Canada did its patriotic duty by selling wheat to the allies, particularly to Great Britain, at several dollars under the world price. The compensation to farmers was never paid. Farmers received several hundreds of millions of dollars less for their wheat during that period of time than they would have if it was sold on the world market. This was probably a valuable and necessary contribution to the war effort, but it was not spread over the entire nation. It fell to farmers to contribute to the war effort.
After the war an agreement was made between the Canadian government and the British government to supply wheat to Britain at fixed prices. At that time it seemed to be a fairly likely and acceptable agreement. However, because of the fluctuation in prices neither Canada nor Britain honoured the agreement. But this agreement spawned the Two-Price Wheat Act we are discussing today.
It takes so long between the time an idea comes to the government and an act is passed that things change greatly. The agreement was supposed to guarantee farmers the cost of production of grain on the export market as well as on the domestic market, but it did neither of those things. The Two-Price Wheat Act only guaranteed a floor price and a ceiling price for wheat sold to the domestic market.
Sometimes floor and ceiling prices work well. They worked well when the price of grain was within those two areas, but when the world price exceeded the ceiling price farmers ended up subsidizing consumers. Until the price levels were changed last year, that subsidy again cost farmers a substantial amount. I noticed that last Friday, as reported in Hansard, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) referred to an amount of approximately $1 million per week as the subsidy by farmers to consumers of bread in Canada. Again farmers paid.
Just lately there was an embargo on the sale of grain to Russia. Again farmers had to pay. In the process of paying compensation because of the embargo hopefully we have established one fact for all time, and that is that when a group of people such as farmers do something which is the responsibility of all Canada, they will not have to pay for it themselves as the farmers did during the Second World War. At least we established the fact that when one acts for all Canada one should be compensated in some way. However, the farmers paid again. This time they were paid the meagre compensation the government decided to pay after 17 months of doing
Two-Price Wheat Act
nothing or very little. The amount was probably less than half the actual losses of the farmers during that period of time.
The Canadian Wheat Board has a mandate from Parliament to obtain the best possible price for farmers' grain. This is done with farmers' money. No taxpayers' money goes to the Wheat Board to provide this service, either domestically or internationally. The Two-Price Wheat Act does not allow the Wheat Board to fulfil its mandate. Legislation such as this confines its ability to obtain the best possible return for farmers.
At present Canadian farmers are being attacked in many areas. They cannot afford to pay a subsidy for the actions of government, for the benefit of consumers, or for the war effort. They could not afford to pay in the past, they cannot afford to pay now, and the way things are going they will not be able to pay in the future. There is an attack on the basic farming or agricultural industry which is affecting the incomes of farmers.
A great effort is being made on the part of many organizations, some of which are very closely attached to the grain industry, to do something about the Crow rate. Most people feel that the rate should be increased to a compensatory rate, which would again make the farmers pay. The situation is such that the industry is barely making enough profit to survive. This is happening in the grain industry as well as in the pork and beef industries. These factors make a considerable difference in the incomes of farmers and can put them out of business.
Also there was a great attack on the marketing boards which were established in the agricultural industry, many of them by this particular government. This attack suggests that the agricultural industry should return to the free marketing system in all areas. Nowhere else in the country is any industry on a free market basis. The idea of supply and demand went out many years ago. No industry with a union goes out and asks how much one will work for. The unions establish the amount paid for a particular job through negotiation. No manufacturer of automobiles would establish its price by producing a million automobiles, putting them on the market and asking buyers: "How much will you pay for this automobile?", regardless of how much it cost the manufacturer.
If we eliminate marketing boards, what we are asking the farmer to do is to produce his grain, produce his meat or whatever product he has, put it on the market and say, "Regardless of what it costs, give me what you think you can afford, or what you want to afford." We have had a very broad attack on marketing boards. We have also had an attack on farmers' income in the form of closing down of rail lines across the west. Many farmers could expect to deliver their grain to a centre which was only six or eight miles from their farms. By the process of closing down the rail lines, a process which is sanctioned by this government, farmers must now haul that grain 25 or 30 miles with increased fuel and mechanical costs.

Two-Price Wheat Act
Therefore, in all of these areas, the farmer, the grain producer, is in a situation which is increasing his costs of production, with no guarantee that he will be paid for those increases. Then we ask him to subsidize the consumer as well.
I have nothing against subsidizing the consumer, particularly the person at the lower end of the income bracket who is unable to buy bread at a high cost. However, we should not ask the farmer to do this as part of his contribution to Canada. He must at least expect to recover the cost of production.
Hence, although I recognize that this bill, which should have been brought forward and passed three years ago, is probably a necessity, it should only be dealt with in the light of the real problems in grain production across the nation; not only the problems in the west for farmers operating under the Canadian Wheat Board, but also the problems of farmers who are producing grain all across the country.

subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I read Bill S-6, by which the government wants to repeal the 1974 act, a saying which was quite common in the west a few years ago and is still common came to mind. There were four professional people, a minister, a lawyer, a doctor and a farmer, who were making brief statements as to what they did for the people. The lawyer said in his brief statement, "I plead for all"; and the crowd clapped. The doctor said, "I prescribe for all"; and the crowd clapped. The minister said, "I pray for all"; and the crowd clapped a little more enthusiastically. Then the farmer's turn came, and his simple statement was, "1 pay for all". There was not any clapping.
This bill illustrates, in a very definite way, how the farmer is always at-excuse the expression-the dirty end of the stick. The farmer is the backbone of this country. Without the farmer we would have no food. Yet, as has been pointed out by a number of hon. members, including my colleague who just sat down, there is no other industry which pays full price for everything it buys but which has no say in regard to the price of the produce that it sells.
It is really amazing why agriculture has continued to grow. It is not surprising that many smaller farmers, particularly those starting operation, are going into bankruptcy because of this very tight squeeze. This bill is another example of a western resource being sold at less than world price. At no time has the farmer in western Canada paid less than full price for his combines, for his tractors, for his trucks or for his cars. At no time has the farmer in western Canada paid less than full price for fish or manufactured goods from the east. As a matter of fact, he paid more than his full price on many occasions because of subsidization and tariffs which make it necessary for the western farmer to pay far more for his shoes and clothes than he would normally have to, were there no high tariffs protecting the clothing and the shoe industry.
But the farmer never seems to have any protection. When we are working out tariffs in Geneva, what do we give? We invariably give something which is of value to the farmer to get something else which is of value to all the people. During the hard times in Britain at the beginning of the Second World War, the Canadian government had the brilliant idea of
sending the people of Britain a million bushels of wheat, I believe. The people of Canada were excited about the imaginative project of sending this food to people in Britain, who were almost singlehandedly at that time fighting against totalitarianism, communism and fascism and having a very tough time. But to make a long story short, that food was not a gift from Canada; it was a gift from the wheat farmers of Canada. They were never reimbursed for that wheat. The people of Britain thanked Canada, but they should have thanked the farmers of Canada because it was the farmers who gave that gift to those people.
Never have the farmers paid less for freight. As a matter of fact, we pay more than our fair share. At one time the price of freight was so ridiculous that we would ship things from Toronto to Vancouver and back to Calgary because we could do it cheaper than shipping it straight from Toronto to Calgary. If anyone from grade one up can see any logic in that, I would like to see him stand up in shame. However, that is what happened. Gradually we got to the point where that situation was eliminated. However, the farmer still pays full price to send his wool to the east and full price to buy the garments back afterwards on the freight. The farmer is not a cry baby; but these matters are lurking at the very heart of our agricultural industry. We are always waiting for solutions, but the solution never seems to come.

subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
This bill would repeal the two-price wheat system. Perhaps the reason the Liberals are becoming so excited is that this legislation would eliminate the obligation of
July 6, 1981

the government to make subsidy payments in accordance with the Two-Price Wheat Act. This was stopped in 1978 yet the bill has still not been passed. We ask our people outside to obey the law. It is almost time for the government to start obeying the law. Until this legislation is passed, the present act is still law. The government knows that.
In 1978 the Canadian Wheat Board regulations established a minimum and a maximum price for wheat for human domestic consumption. The senator in charge of the Wheat Board announced a minimum price of $5 and a maximum price of $7 per bushel of wheat for human consumption. There was no maximum for durum wheat. I would like to know why there is a maximum for any kind of wheat. Why is the government deciding that $7 will be the maximum price for wheat? I do not see any maximum price for electricity which goes from eastern Canada to the United States. I do not see any maximum or minimum payments for coal which we import from the United States while leaving our Canadian mines idle. Why are we setting a maximum and a minimum price for wheat, particularly a maximum price? The previous minimum was $3.25 per bushel, yet the world price during that time went up to $6 or $7, and perhaps even higher. Who took the loss? The western wheat growers took the loss.
The people of Canada are being subsidized by the benevolent government which uses the money which should go into the pockets of the farmers. That is exactly what happened. We are now setting a maximum price at $7 a bushel. Why should there be a maximum price at all? If the world price goes up to $10, why should our farmers not receive that? You do not see anyone outside our country putting down their prices for the commodities we buy. Oil on the world market sells for between $40 and $50 per barrel while the price we pay to western Canada is $18 per barrel. What is fair about that? Now we are trying to do the same thing to our farmers. It does not matter what the wheat price goes to in the world market, our farmers will not receive more than $7 unless they are growing durum wheat. Surely any hon. member would agree that is not fair. If a maximum price is to be established, surely the cost of production plus a reasonable profit should be taken into consideration.
If that were the case then the situation would have to be flexible since costs of production change every year. This year costs are rising. They are rising due to actions of governments, including this one, which placed an excise tax on natural gas and raised the price of fertilizer, which in turn causes the cost of production to rise. Many people pleaded with the government to remove that excise tax because it affected production. The government said that it would stick with it, and stick with it it did.
If there is to be a maximum and minimum price for wheat, then it should not be confined to the farmers of Canada. Why is the government not trying to work out a definite arrangement with the Americans since Canada and the U.S. ship about 65 per cent or 70 per cent of their wheat to the markets of the world? There is no use trying to undercut each other. A few years ago Premier Lougheed made a trip to Russia and
Two-Price Wheat Act
found out that we were playing second fiddle to the United States with regard to wheat sales. We only sold wheat when we beat the Americans at the bargaining table and the Premier of Alberta, who represented a number of farmers, did not like that. Later on I went to the Wheat Board and discussed this matter with the people there. They did not like the idea of Premier Lougheed going to Russia and talking about the price of wheat. I told them that I thought they should be happy about that and that every premier in Canada sould take an interest in the price their producers are receiving and try to get them a better one.
If the American and Canadian governments got together and established a price under which we will not sell-

subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: We do not want a cartel. We want something which will give the producer his cost of production plus a reasonable profit. That is all we want. The minister's government is prepared to accept oil from a cartel, a real cartel which places no emphasis whatsoever on the costs of production. It does not cost $50 a barrel to produce oil or anything like that. An artificial price is set at what the market will bear. The government is prepared to use that oil instead of our own at 75 per cent of the price. We are not asking for a cartel. We are asking that the price take into consideration the cost of production plus a reasonable profit. I say to the minister that there is no other industry in Canada which would not expect the same thing. But every industry, if it is to stay in business, must obtain its cost of production and a reasonable profit.

subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND

We are not trying hard enough. The minister may be trying, but is the senator in charge of the Wheat Board trying? He is spending a great deal of time on prosecuting the farmers instead of trying to get something for them, as I will show in a minute. Instead of trying to get something for the farmers he is prosecuting them with their own money.
If we must establish a price, then let us not establish it just for Canadians. Let us establish a price which is reasonable and sensible, one which will be flexible so that the costs of production can be included as they change. I would wager that 90 per cent of the farmers, if not 100 per cent, would jump for joy if the government would do just that. It is amazing that the farmers have been able to stay in business up until now. They only do so because of the family farm. The wife goes out and looks after the hens, the kids gather the eggs and the grandparents go out and pick berries. That is how farmers survive. Do not think that they are rich people. They not only work eight hours a day, but 12 or 14, and sometimes right around the clock during harvest and seeding time. They work hard for what they receive and all they are asking for is a reasonable price-the cost of production plus a reasonable profit.
I believe it was the last member who spoke who said something about the producers providing a subsidy of some $20 million to the consumers since the price was locked in at

July 6, 1981
Two-Price Wheat Act
$5 per bushel. Many farmers are becoming very disgruntled about this situation. They are tired of waiting. I would say 99 per cent of them want to stay in Canada but they want to receive a fair deal too. But they are becoming frustrated and no one seems to listen. When we talk about a fair price for crops, members on the government benches begin to heckle. I do not know why they should be so against the farmer. A lot of these farmers came from Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes. They worked hard for what they built up. They built a heritage and they want to stay in Canada. I think this country should take definite steps to give them a decent standard of living. They should be paid their cost of production plus a reasonable profit.
Some people may ask what a reasonable profit is. It is said that a reasonable profit for the banks is now 19 per cent or 20 per cent. I would be amazed if the farmers want that much, but why should they not? When the banks get 20 per cent profit on loans of money, why should the farmers not get 20 per cent for producing food for the people of this country and the world? That could be negotiated and the farmers would be prepared to negotiate. The bill is still in the House, Mr. Speaker, and I think some payment should be made to the farmers up until it is repealed. We simply should not say, "We started this in 1978, so we are not going to pay anything after 1978."
I should like to come to another point, Mr. Speaker. I want to emphasize that the cost of production should be flexible. The $5 and the $3.25 prices have been in effect for seven years. During that period other prices have gone up but not the price of wheat. The farmers still cannot get more than $5 per bushel. They are not asking for a rip-off but for a price that will cover the cost of production plus a reasonable profit. They want it to be flexible and they want it to take into account the items that contribute to the cost of production.
According to information which comes from the Canadian Wheat Board, farmers do not know whether to grow wheat or barley or rye or flax because they do not know what the price of these crops will be until well into the crop year. They are not told two months ahead of time so that they can make plans. I can tell hon. members that no one knows better than the farmer what he should grow on his land. There may be brains at the Wheat Board in Winnipeg and in Ottawa, but it is the farmer who knows what his land should produce. If he knew before the beginning of the crop year what the price of the various crops would be, he could make his decision on whether to grow barley or wheat, say.
I want to deal now with something that I consider to be a national disgrace. I believe the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) has left the House and will likely be back shortly. 1 would urge him to use his influence in connection with the problems with wheat storage. We had bumper crops in 1978 throughout the west, particularly in the Stavely area. As a result, there was a shortage of storage and the farmers would
have had to pile their wheat and barley on the ground, which would have resulted in a 10 per cent loss of wheat.
It happened that the Alberta Wheat Pool elevator in Stavely had room for all the quotas and then had room to spare, so the agent took the grain in for storage. He did not have a quota but was simply going to store it so that the farmers would not have to pile it in the fields. He had enough space for all the quotas and made a monthly rental charge for storage in accordance with the rules of the Wheat Board. I think any reasonable man would say that was a sensible thing to do, but the bureaucrats in the Canadian Wheat Board had some regulations to enforce. They considered this to be an illegal act, on the grounds that any grain in an elevator over and above the quota is an average and is illegal, even if storage tickets have been issued and charges levied and paid.
As a result, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Wheat Board, a farmer-owned organization, charged 53 farmers because they dared arrange for storage in an Alberta Wheat Pool farmer-owned elevator to protect their grain. The Canadian Wheat Board then seized all the permit books and commenced legal proceedings. The local wheat pool supervisor told the agent that he was at liberty to issue cheques for the grain but the people who stored 70,000 bushels of barley were not paid for several months. Each farmer was summoned to appear in court, as was the elevator agent. This was a case where a farmer body, established to aid in the equitable sale of grain, rode roughshod over the producer to whom they were responsible. It did not bother the Canadian Wheat Board that adequate storage was available; it did not bother the Canadian Wheat Board that the elevator was accepting payment or that storage tickets had been issued.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on the Two-Price Wheat Act, I can state firsthand that the farmers of western Canada are not happy with pricing and the way the government is handling the two-price wheat system. It is interesting to note that there are a couple of commodities which come under the two-price system, one being wheat, which we are dealing with in Bill S-6, and the other oil. Both of these commodities come from a certain area of the country. At very great expense, both benefit the part of
July 6, 1981

the country from which the minister who just spoke comes. Therefore, he can well get up in this House and defend his actions with vigour.
However, if he would speak to the farmers in western Canada about the two-price system and the fact that down through the years it has taken millions of dollars out of their pockets while they have had to pay full price for every commodity they bought from industrial Canada, and often at many more times the price, he would find the attitude is quite different from what he perceived it to be today, particularly as it relates to wheat and the cost of production, as related by my colleague from Alberta.
We in western Canada are very serious about this situation. If the federal government is going to put in place a productive system which will bring about increased production of wheat for the benefit of Canadians and others throughout the world, it had better start bringing in positive legislation, not this kind. I see the minister has left the chamber.
It is important that the government know what is happening. Should the western Canadian farmer be called upon to subsidize other consumers in Canada? They are willing to do that to a point, but they believe that all Canadians should accept that responsibility, not only the farmers of western Canada.
The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) stated in the debate last Friday that this is costing the farmers in western Canada up to a million dollars a week. This is unacceptable and should be changed. The same is happening with regard to oil. Western Canadians receive $18.75 a barrel with the $1 increase on July 1. However, there are some good terms. There is the "blended price", the "compensation price", and the $43 a barrel price that is paid to Mexico and to OPEC. There is a two-price system, one for western Canada and one for offshore oil coming into this country.
The same is happening in the wheat industry. It is very relevant how western Canadians perceive fairness as a result of the federal government's actions. How long can this go on? Western farmers are productive. At one time the farmers made up 97 per cent of the population of North America. Today they make up less than 5 per cent of the population. They produce enough to feed all of North America and a good part of the rest of the world.
If this government continues to bring in this kind of legislation as it relates to wheat, there will be the same production situation that we now have in the oil industry in western Canada. That is what will happen if the government is not careful. It is time the government did something positive for the grain farmers.
What has the cost been to the farmer? We all know the cost of production. 1 read in the Toronto Star today about a farmer who is going broke because the interest payments on his farm are $8,000 more than his gross income. This is a situation that must be looked at very seriously. What is happening when farmers must purchase tractors, machinery, equipment and so on? The farmer must pay full price and
Two-Price Wheat Act
often a protected price for the commodity. He could bring in a small John Deere tractor from West Germany at quite a saving. This is because the government protects the industrial area of Canada.
When it comes to selling wheat, who does the government protect? It protects the same people at the expense of the farmer. The farmer must pay when he buys and pay again when he sells. Are the farmers satisfied with this situation? No.
I should not be political about this, but there was a good example on the weekend. The NDP had a little meeting in Vancouver. It came through loud and clear that a segment of the NDP are not satisfied with what is going on in this House and with the centralist control which dominates oil, wheat and the lives of Canadians. The convention in Vancouver should give the message to those in government that there are some pretty clear thinking people in western Canada. They have very strong views on such issues as the Canada Wheat Act and the amendments with regard to the two-price system.
The western farmer is asking how long can this go on? How long can he continue to pay the high prices plus a subsidy to industry on everything he buys? When he sells, it is at a low price. How can he pay his bills and stay in business? Bankruptcies are up. I mentioned earlier the high interest rates. This is related to the cost of production for the farmer. Pressures on the farmer have never been greater. They are closing in. Bankruptcies are higher than ever before.
If this situation continues, by next spring many more young farmers will be faced with bankruptcies. They will not be able to maintain a fluid financial position. I ask the government to take a good look at this situation. The laxity in bringing forward this bill is a good indication of the type of direction the government has taken in relation to important agricultural issues.
How important is agriculture to Canada and the world? It is interesting to note that for one hundred years or better the economic power structure of the world has been controlled by the manufacturing sector which operates in Toronto, Montreal, eastern Canada and also places like London, England, Paris, Tokyo and so forth. This sector has controlled the economy of the world. Along came OPEC. I see someone frowning and wondering how relevant this is. It is very relevant because it affects the existence of the farmer. What happened? Along came OPEC, and the economic control of the world switched to the production of energy in certain parts of the world. In Canada that part happens to be western Canada, and central Canada does not like that at all.
The next thing which will happen in the world is that there will be some emphasis put on the production of food-wheat- which is what we are talking about here. If we in this House or the government take the attitude toward the production of wheat that has been taken in this House in the past year-in the short time I have been in the House-and toward agriculture and farmers generally, it will be a sorry day for Canada and a sorry day for the world.

July 6, 1981
Two-Price Wheat Act
We must allow the farmer in western Canada to make his contribution to this great country. This is a great country. We have many things. We have energy. We have manufacturing here in eastern Canada. We in the west need eastern cars, steel and rubber, and we can work together. We in western Canada are good Canadians. All we are asking is that we be given a fair chance. We are not asking for two oil prices, one domestic and one for the international marketplace. We do not want a domestic price for wheat and another price for the export market which is $2 or $3 higher. We want a fair price. Let us not put a limit of $7 on wheat when the price could go to $10. Let us be fair. The western farmer will produce wheat and the industrial area of Canada will produce cars and steel. The energy sector of Canada will start producing oil again, as it has not been doing for a year and a half because of the policies of this government. We can build the strongest country in all the world, and that country is Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the whole country is aware that the books around here are in some difficulty. We are aghast that this kind of action has not come before the House sooner than it has. The general principle is what I am referring to here, a principle to which I am opposed.

subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to participate in this amendment to the original Two-Price Wheat Act. Last Friday the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) in his opening remarks indicated that this is the fourth time Bill S-6 has come before this House in its present state. He reminded us of that and that the last debate took place almost exactly one year ago. I think it would be a year ago tomorrow. The most obvious and succinct comment which now seems appropriate is that the bill itself is now 15 months out of date since its first reading, which actually took place on April 16, 1980.
At the time of those earlier debates there was general agreement that wheat producers were locked into what has been termed by others a frozen seven-year contract under the
original terms of the act and, further, that the two-price wheat system has been a subsidy to consumers at the expense of producers. I think that is now widely accepted by all concerned. That subsidy favours the consumer because of the rapid increase in farm production costs associated with our record rate of inflation and I suggest there has been a disproportionate increase in farm capital and operating costs as compared with other sectors in our society with respect to how inflation affects them.
I do not think there is any doubt that farmers are taking the brunt of inflation more so than other sectors, although the whole economy is certainly involved. This situation has increased the imbalance of this subsidy in favour of consumers at the expense of the wheat producers.
Here are just a few examples of how this is reacting today. Fuel costs at the farm level have now more than doubled. Commercial fertilizer costs have increased in direct ratio to those for the oil and natural gas which are used to produce most commercial fertilizers. In some instances insufficient amounts of fertilizer were used this spring simply because of the inability of well-established farmers to finance those very high costs for fertilizer. The very high land and machinery costs with 20 per cent and sometimes higher interest rates, with no sign of let-up, are perhaps the most critical and crucial cost factors which are today precipitating bank foreclosures and bankruptcies at alarming rates. Wheat producers must get a more equitable share of this subsidy.
I would like now to make a comment about the general conditions of grain production, crop prospects and, even more than that, general growth, including grass and hay in western Canada, because I think this is very important as we head into the hot weather part of the summer, rapid growth, the heading out of our crops, haying and so on. I am sure hon. members in this House will recall my personal concerns early last spring and again a year ago last spring, in 1980, when I was genuinely concerned about what to me was the potential for very serious drought throughout western Canada, especially on the western prairies. I spoke in this House, in the Standing Committee on Agriculture and in the Standing Committee on Regional Development about the PFRA and about these concerns. They were very real indeed because there was a potential for drought following two successive winter droughts where the whole of the western prairies had a very low snowfall. As a consequence there was a very poor to nil snow run-off. In the spring of 1980 and the spring of 1981, over a vast area, there was no run-off to supply soil moisture not only for growth but also for livestock watering purposes, and hundreds, perhaps thousands, of small flood schemes used to produce feed for livestock.
I would say that today all the earlier concern and pessimism, certainly on my part, is gone thanks to generous rains over the last six weeks in most of the prairie provinces. In just six weeks the situation has corrected itself to where we now have a rather fantastic turnaround in total growth across the prairies
July 6, 1981

and the possibility of still further growth in production is there.
Last Saturday 1 drove the 160 miles from where I live at Walsh, on the Saskatchewan border, to west of Warner, which is in southwestern Alberta. In fact, I drove pretty well across the southern part of Alberta, ending up in the vicinity of what is known as the Milk River ridge. This is beautiful country with a high ridge which is noted for the quality and high production of grass and hay. As a result we have the wonderful cattle and horse ranches which have their headquarters there. I would say without hesitation that the present growth of prairie grass over the whole area, indeed over a much wider area, is the best I have seen since 1953. At that time we had a wonderful rain which coincided with the coronation of the present Queen. It lasted for several days and is still known as the coronation rain. Well, the growth conditions we now have equal or exceed those conditions back in 1953.
I would say many varieties of native grasses are two feet tall and already setting seed. They are high enough to completely hide young calves walking through it. Hay supplies, in spite of the lack of spring run-off, will be adequate. Cereal grain production possibilities are equally good with many fields now fully headed out, and that is spring seeding. The potential for cereal grain production as well as the grasses I mentioned is enormous. Naturally, it is a long way from being in the bin but there is a potential for an enormous grain crop throughout the western prairies. There is one area I am told still on the dry side. That is around Lloydminster, along the Saskatchewan-Alberta border. There may also be an area from Moose Jaw south to the Montana border that is equally dry. However, it is my understanding that those areas are now getting rain.
For those of us in Alberta who are becoming accustomed to the change, it is interesting to speculate that the production of barley in Alberta may be at an all time high. That, of course, will lead to the potential for feeding more livestock, notably cattle and hogs, in our various feed lots, and to the export of more barley.
That brings up the whole question of what the initial prices will be when the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board gets together with his advisers and makes the initial announcement. That will have a tremendous amount to do with whether or not barley production in Alberta, combined with a good price, will allow the feed industry to end almost a full year of losses. The supply of barley will be there; it remains to be seen whether the price will be high enough to make it worthwhile for the farmers and the feed industry.
I mention these western grain details to indicate the importance of the initial price, which I think should have been announced long before now. I hope the minister will see fit to bring it forward. Those initial prices for all grains will have to be significantly higher to counter the increased costs I have already commented on.
I want now to come to another aspect, Mr. Speaker. I think all western farmers, no matter what they produce, are concerned that this amendment is simply a device for the government to get out of that $200 million contract, if you like,
Two-Price Wheat Act
which was promised in the original seven-year proposal that the former minister, the Hon. Otto Lang, brought in. I think there is a distrust among the prairie farmers as to whether the government will live up to its commitments. We had a good example of that over the winter, in fact early this spring, some of which is still with us, over the manner in which the government administered the drought program. I am thinking particularly about the herd maintenance program. While the concept was noble and most appropriate, the manner in which it was administered left much to be desired.
I want to have on the record what the situation is today. I suggest that the review board, created late in the day, if you like, to try and iron out some of these administrative inequities, is hopefully going to do just that by its decisions. My understanding is that the review board, just before being disbanded as being no longer required by the responsible ministers, had indicated some 3,600 unsatisfied claims for herd maintenance payments which they split into four categories. Categories one and two were the most extreme and covered cattle producers most severely hit. Categories three and four were those with a smaller percentage of cattle in their operations and a larger percentage of grain. It is my understanding there were as many as 3,000 producers in categories one and two.
Now, when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) set up this review board, he gave a commitment on behalf of the government that individuals who felt they were not being fairly dealt with would be able to have their cases brought before the review board. Failing that, the minister would respond personally to them. I suggest that there is at least 2,500 to 3,000 cases where the government has made a commitment to stand behind its promise in the drought program. There is no question that there is a carryover of money available to do this, but no action has yet been taken.
Primarily I want to zero in on a small area on the Alberta side. Generally it is the area on the south side of the Cypress Hills. It is right on the Alberta-Saskatchewan boundary. It is approximately five or six ranges wide and about eight or nine townships running north from the Montana border to almost the top of the Cypress Hills. This area was every bit as seriously hit by the drought last summer and last winter, as well as the previous summer and winter, as any area in the west but it was not recognized under the program.
I must say quite candidly that it now appears the reason the area was not recognized was that perhaps it had the misfortune under the program to be on the Alberta side. It is the only reason I can see that the area was not recognized under the program. It is a tragedy in the way a program can be administered.
The Minister of Agriculture is aware of this. I hope there is still time to do something about it. The people in the area are widely scattered-there are not too many-but they have been required to finance enormous bills in order to purchase feed to get them through the last two winters. Indeed they are worthy

July 6, 1981
Two-Price Wheat Act
of some consideration, in light of the firm commitment of the Government of Canada to do something about the emergency drought situation.
Before concluding my remarks I want to make one more point. I have enlarged upon the total potential for a great quantity of grain in the west. It will pinpoint more than ever before the need for the federal government and various feed grain and agricultural groups in western Canada to make a genuine effort to get together and try to reach a compromise solution of the Crow freight rate dilemma. There is no doubt that there is widespread support for some changes across the western prairies. There seems to be stronger support in the provinces of Alberta and Manitoba, but even in the province of Saskatchewan-I live very close to that province and I winter a lot of my cattle there, so I keep in touch-there is the beginning of a consensus as to how to resolve who receives the Crow benefit, that is, the difference between the actual amount of the Crow freight rates and the compensatory rates, or the necessary rates for the railways to move the grain and make a reasonable profit. There is widespread agreement that the railways must be much better compensated, but there is no agreement as to what system should be used, how much, or how it is to be paid out.
The western agricultural conference group proposed that the Crow benefit be paid directly to the railways. The commodity coalition group, the users of mostly feed grains in cattle or hog production and the processors of rapeseed, made a proposal that the difference between the two levels of compensation to the railways should be paid directly to farmers or producers on an acreage basis. It would remove the need to identify grain, multiplying it by a per bushel price.
There is evidence that those two groups are getting closer to reaching compromise. The federal government might very well encourage that compromise. They should get together in order to resolve this situation. There will be record grain volumes to move. We think we are making headway with new hopper cars, but they will not begin to move the expected increase in grain production in the prairies. If the commodity groups do not have a sense of satisfaction that their case in the Crow rate issue is understood, we will lose an opportunity all over western Canada to come up with the best market possible for the barley which is being grown out there right now. Of course, the best market is on the farm next door to where it is produced or on the same farm; there is no doubt about that.
Throughout this year barley was fed to hogs and cattle, and cattlemen ended up losing $100 per head for every fat steer. This did not happen throughout the entire year but it did occur. Hog producers are only now beginning to do a little better. If the secondary industry which creates much of the labour in spin-off industries such as the packing plants does not feel it is worth its while, the grain transportation authority will have to move the extra barley, or a substantial part of it, into the export market. If it is looked upon in that light, it is only common sense and good business to come to a compromise on the Crow issue. I am sure a compromise can be reached by those two major western groups.
I know Mr. Speaker may feel that I have wandered slightly from the subject of the Two-Price Wheat Act, but it was appropriate to make comments about the crop prospects in western Canada since they have turned around so dramatically and to relate that to the entire question of the Crow rate dilemma which is of major concern to us all.
While we appear to have resolved the grain car situation through the construction of hopper cars which are paid for either by the grain producers, through the Canadian Wheat Board, or by the taxpayers of Canada, there is a disturbing situation on the railways with respect to special livestock cars which are rapidly becoming obsolete. It seems that both railways have a mathematical formula whereby after so many years stock cars officially become obsolete. They are not being replaced at this time. The railways indicate quite bluntly that it is not worth their while. This is not because of the Crow rate subsidy. The owners of all livestock carried by rail pay the full shot. There is no subsidized freight rate for livestock, but the railways feel it is not worth their while to continue to pay for new cars to replace the obsolete ones. The livestock industry is very concerned about this situation. It is part and parcel of the uneasiness in western Canadian agriculture which some positive action by the federal government could do much to alleviate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members opposite will not even allow me to refer to that ancient document, the Speech from the Throne, which has been before us for 18 months. What did that Speech from the Throne point out? Among other things, at the very end of it there was a passing reference to some of the problems which face the government with respect to its representation in western Canada. In that document there was a request made to members of the opposition that at every opportunity we should bring to the government's attention the concerns, grievances, hopes and aspirations of the people of western Canada. The bill before us allows us the opportunity to point out in very vivid and specific terms some of the problems which face the western farmer at a time of unprecedented inflation and at a time when interest rates are punishing the western farmer as he has never been punished before.
In effect, we are talking about the western farmer subsidizing the consumers of Canada with respect to the price of wheat which is grown in western Canada, which is where this bill will have its greatest impact. The price of grain is a matter of ongoing concern to western Canadians and to farmers. This bill shows the kind of disinterest which this government has toward western Canada. When that is combined with the lack of action of this government and with other unconscionable delays which have taken place in terms of payments to which western farmers are entitled, there can be no doubt of this government's disinterest. We had to wait until the last few days for a statement from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) with respect to payment of the Soviet grain embargo compensation. By the time the government found it within its priorities to make that announcement, the amount of back payment had been substantially depreciated by the ravages of inflation and the loss of interest to the farmer on this money. Quite frankly, western farmers looked at that payment with the utmost skepticism.
Simply put, this bill is also an indication of the kind of treatment that western farmers receive at the hands of this government. There are a number of opportunities which members from western Canada have to bring to the attention of the government certain improvements which could take place in terms of its legislation. We intend to take advantage of those opportunities and to meet that challenge. The point is, not only do we have that responsibility, which we will carry out, but we have been called upon by the government in its Speech from

July 6, 1981
Two-Price Wheat Act
the Throne to articulate the points of view of western Canadians.
Hopefully, the government will take some of these suggestions into consideration. There have been a number of agriculture programs introduced by the Liberal government regarding which we have made suggestions. The western grain stabilization program is one, which was brought in by the then minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, Mr. Otto Lang. We suggested a number of ways in which that particular program might be improved so that there would be, in effect, some benefit derived by western farmers. Those suggestions were rejected out of hand by the Liberal government.

The reason I wish to make this point is that it must be looked at in the context of this government's agricultural policies. The fact of the matter is that the relevance here is 100 per cent. We made some suggestions about how western grain stabilization could be improved. For example, the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton) suggested that the payments to the western farmers should be made on an individual basis, that there should be individual plans rather than having it apply to the designated
Wheat Board area in western Canada. At the very minimum, we suggested this improvement to the bill. We suggested that we have smaller and more coherent districts so that there would be a triggering of the payments to western farmers; but the government refused to listen. As a result, what happened? Western Canadian farmers have been deprived of any payments under that legislation, because unless there is a complete crop failure across the whole of western Canada, the plan does not go into effect.
This particular legislation is another example of the way in which the western farmer is again asked to reduce his income; because he has been asked, by the provisions of this bill, to subsidize the consumer in Canada with respect to the price of wheat consumed domestically.
My colleague the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) brought forward some of the concerns we had about the herd maintenance program. I will not get into that; Your Honour listened to the hon. member for Medicine Hat make a very excellent presentation indeed about that particular program. However, things are so bad now with the Liberal government respecting this particular program which, as my colleague pointed out, has a minimum of some 3,600 unsatisfied claims before the review board, that now when I write to the Minister of Agriculture, who is holding himself out as some kind of spokesman in the House of Commons for western Canadian farmers, he is now saying that he has nothing further to do with the western herd maintenance program, and would I please send my objections, my concerns, my complaints and my constituents' complaints to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. De Bane). That is what I call backing off from one's responsibilities as a minister of agriculture. That is the attitude the government is taking. It knows that the western farmer is unhappy with the policies of this government.
Now I want to deal with the provisions of the legislation. I want to deal with some specific concerns and complaints that I have about it. Your Honour will remember that the bill which we have before us repeals the Two-Price Wheat Act of 1974. The two-price wheat system has, in fact, established a system intended to run for seven years. At the time the original bill was introduced, our party took a firm stand against the length of that particular provision. I will deal with that particular matter a little later. The parliamentary secretary, who is one of the two western Canadian hon. members, should be interested in finding out how this bill could be improved.
As a matter of fact, at the time, our party moved an amendment to this original legislation to reduce the time and the application of this particular provision from seven years, which is an unconscionably long period of time. At that time it was pointed out that no labour organization or union would agree to commit themselves for a period of seven years. Nowadays the unions will go six months to a year in terms of any contract they may enter into. Yet the western farmer, by virtue of the policy of the Liberal government, is committed to a seven-year term with respect to this whole program.

I should point out that that particular amendment on behalf of our party was brought forward by the Hon. Jack Horner, who is known to the government benchers. The fact is that at that time his thinking in terms of policy was clear, before he moved across the way. I compliment the Hon. Jack Horner for a motion that he made on the amendment to this bill. The only answer that I have seen thus far with respect to trying to deal with western problems and concerns, is apparently the candidacy now announced of Jim Coutts, who, of course, was instrumental in bringing Jack Horner across to the Liberal party. We now have someone in the Liberal party with sex appeal. Jim Coutts is now going to speak on behalf of the western farmer. I am very impressed, and I ask Your Honour whether that is the only answer the government has with respect to this bill.

There was a $5 per bushel ceiling for red spring wheat. As far as durum was concerned, it was $5.75 a bushel and $7.50 a bushel on the lower and higher ends. Millers and consumers of grain for human and domestic purposes purchased the wheat at the floor price. Of course, the intention of the original legislation was that the government pay to the Wheat Board the difference between the floor and the world price, up to a maximum of $1.75 per bushel. In other words, $3.25 was the minimum price, and adding $1.75 made $5. I mention that only because when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) was in Vancouver, he paid a bill for $120, added a $20 tip, and totalled that up to $130. I just want to make sure that the Liberals, who are in charge of our financial affairs, understand simple addition. Apparently this was not the case with former ministers of finance.
In the fall of 1978, the government decided to terminate payments under the act. At the same time, a new scheme- that is, $4 minimum and $5 maximum-was introduced through regulations made under the Canadian Wheat Board.
I am pleased to see that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is here because I think it is important for him to participate and be in the House at all times when bills relating to Wheat Board problems and questions are debated on the floor of the House. One of the difficulties we have, of course, as the minister knows, is that the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board is not a member of this chamber. It makes it very difficult when the minister involved is not here to participate in the debate and answer questions and to have input from western Canadian members.
We have an assistant minister who has other responsibilities. I am glad that he is here to participate, and I welcome him to the chamber. I appreciate the fact that he is here, because I
