The minister keeps talking about adjustment. What we are talking about now is legislation that would legalize something that was done illegally in 1978 by the Liberal government. By what kind of logic would the minister suggest that adjustments have been made when the bill provided no opportunity for such adjustments? There was no provision in the legislation for an adjustment over and above the price which was subsequently changed because of enormous pressure put on the Liberal government in 1978 as the result of the world price for grain. The Liberal government acted then without consulting Parliament. It acted illegally and that is the whole thrust of my argument. This is a critical problem in the present environment.
From 1973 to 1979, including the second quarter, the index of crop production expenses rose by 105.5 per cent; the cost of agricultural chemicals increased by 168 per cent; and the cost of fertilizer rose by roughly 120 per cent. You look surprised and horrified at these figures, Mr. Speaker, but this is the case. A system which fails to recognize such changes in production costs is clearly deficient. A lack of responsiveness to changing conditions creates subsidy effects that are unintended and undesirable.
For example, during the first four months of the 1979-80 crop year, the grain price in the international market was above the maximum level provided by the two-price system. The result was that grain growers, in western Canada primarily, provided a subsidy of about $1 million per week. This is unfair and is totally unacceptable. It is a system that would not be tolerated in any other context, but the government does not seem inclined to take it seriously or to remedy it, except through periodic and understandable outbursts from the Postmaster General. For the first time in his career he had spoken on an agricultural bill, even though it was under the guise of a point of order.
Even though the world price has often been as much as S2 per bushel higher than the $5 maximum established in 1973, the government did nothing for years. The record is clear on that. Only recently has it seen fit to announce a modified price range based on a $5 per bushel minimum and a $7 per bushel maximum for spring wheat.
This adjustment does not address the basic problem about which I have been speaking. There must be a provision for regular adjustments in price, otherwise production costs and fluctuating world prices will create, and it is likely to be sooner than later, the same type of distortions and problems that arose under the pricing regime that endured from 1973 until just recently.
Since the beginning of this government's mandate it has sat inert and watched wheat producers lose $50 million. We have talked about compensation for losses sustained by grain farmers, but the compensation announced by the minister in the other place responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board amounted to some $68 million. This is roughly the same amount that farmers lost in subsidies before the government made any move. Are the western farmers now supposed to stand up and cheer because they get this $68 million after a year and a half and after inflation has substantially depreciated the amount? They are not going to cheer, Mr. Speaker; they are going to ask what the government is doing on their behalf.
There is no assurance that this same government complacency will not create similar problems as prices shift in the future. There is absolutely no assurance from the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board that the government has any plan to deal with such price fluctuations in the future. There is every likelihood that producers will continue to subsidize consumers. This very day we are looking at prices which are just a few cents below the new ceiling.
The new pricing regime is interesting because it provides no ceiling price for durum wheat. The rationale for the difference between the price-setting policy for hard wheat and durum escapes me. Why should the sky be the limit for one grain and a $7 ceiling be imposed on the other? The same principle should apply to both. There is much to recommend the system that is in place for durum. The lack of a ceiling means, obviously, that rising world prices will not bump through the ceiling while the government is asleep.
That is something that should be considered because there is no plan now for the government to make further adjustments. The western farmer simply has to wait on the pleasure of the government to increase the maximum price and enhance the subsidy on domestically consumed wheat. On the basis of past experience we have no reason to believe that the government will move quickly. Economic conditions and concern about the government's deficit position do not bring the western farmer much hope of priority treatment with respect to this payment. It will be easy for the government not to make an adjustment until some time in the future.
People in Saskatchewan may say that Senator Argue did this and did that, but they also say, "We did not elect Senator Argue. The maximum price should be removed. This, then, becomes a legitimate subsidy to protect the consumer. The situation which has occurred in the past and which is going to occur again in the future as surely as I stand here, where the producer subsidizes the consumer, will be prevented.
We need a viable agricultural industry in our society. That is absolutely essential. Anything that tends to depreciate from that fundamental position I absolutely oppose. I do not believe the two-price system should include a feature that has the effect of forcing producers to subsidize consumers directly. If we as a country decide that grain prices should be subsidized, then the general public should bear the burden of the subsidy. It should not be shouldered only by the producers in one part of the country.
A ceiling price which has no provision for regular adjustment will create such subsidy effects. The government has demonstrated that it cannot react quickly enough to prevent this from happening. Therefore, I submit in all seriousness that there is much to recommend the notion of a no ceiling price. A ceiling price could only be defended if it was linked to a floor price that reflected real costs of production. This is important, and it is one of the reasons the government had to move with respect to a floor price.
Even now, in terms of the costs involved in agricultural production, how can anyone in this House talk about the floor price now in existence as being sufficient to cover the costs of production as far as western farmers are concerned? In that situation I think producers could expect help when prices fell below reasonable levels. And, in return, they would expect to see the top taken off their grain prices in times of high prices. There would be a stabilizing effect whereby both consumers and producers would benefit from time to time.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to address a few remarks to Bill S-6. This is the third time this bill has been introduced. It was introduced first by the previous Liberal administration as Bill C-24, secondly by the PC government as Bill C-7, and thirdly now in the form we see today.
It is interesting to note that the combined Liberal-NDP coalition was in a hurry to bring down the PC government, giving absolutely no thought to the Two-Price Wheat Act at that time. I might say they did not give it even passing interest. That was the coalition of the Liberals and the NDP.
Now the Liberals want to bring this act before us for debate and get it through before the recess. Why is this? Is it because of the magnanimous concern of the Liberal government for the prairie wheat farmer? Is it because of concern for the consumers of Canada? Not quite. It is so that the government can save its own skin. The government will be in trouble if this bill is not passed and the act repealed. The Liberal government would have to pay the producers of western Canada $200 million.
When the Hon. Otto Lang introduced the bill in this House in 1974, he proclaimed, and I quote from page 864 of Hansard for October 29, 1974:
This is a bill whose specific purpose is to enshrine for a period of years, in this case for seven years, a procedure whereby the treasury supplements payments made for wheat designed for human consumption in Canada ... It is in its present form without any doubt and, 1 should think without any argument, in the nature of a consumer subsidy, an amount paid by the treasury, on behalf of the people of Canada as taxpayers, to lighten the burden on the consumer of the cost of wheat products in Canada.
On the passage of that bill the producers in western Canada were locked into a seven-year contract. It was violently opposed by the then Conservative opposition. On May 6, 1975, at page 5538 of Hansard the Hon. Jack Horner said:
This bill locks the wheat producer into a seven-year agreement. 1 cannot overemphasize that. Everyone in this House has witnessed several labour negotiations. I can recite the railway negotiations, the longshoremen on the west coast, grain handlers and longshoremen on the St. Lawrence, and so on. None of them relate to a seven year contract.. . What has this parliament got against wheat producers? Why lock them into a fixed price for their commodity?
I do not hear any comments from the little red rump to my left.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration) moved
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: ADULT OCCUPATIONAL TRAINING ACT, NO. 2 MEASURETO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-67, an Act to amend the Adult Occupational Training Act (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the presentation of this bill introduces a number of very significant amendments to the Adult Occupational Training Act. But before getting into the actual substance of those proposals, I would like to make one short comment about the present situation we face in relation to training. It has been one of the issues which, over the past year or two, has gradually emerged as one of the important public and private priorities across Canada. Increasingly, members of the business community, trade unions, provincial governments and our own government, have focused on the need to substantially increase the availability of skilled workers in Canada as one of the major solutions we can provide to some of the economic problems that we face in this country. It is for this reason that the amendments being presented tonight, I hope, will commend themselves to hon. members of this House for speedy and quick passage.
These amendments are designed to give us the ability to respond, in a flexible and effective way, to many of the concerns which have been registered by Canadians and to the need to substantially improve and upgrade the availability of highly-skilled workers for our industries across Canada.
It is interesting, if one looks at some of the projections, to note that we are going through some major transformations in the labour markets of Canada. For the last 10, 15 or 20 years, what we have been faced with is an increasing need to respond to an expanding labour force. The large numbers of young people coming into the labour market, as well as the increased participation of women, have given us a very strong and increasingly forceful need to supply any kind of job, almost at any price; but those conditions are now changing. The composition of the labour force is now going through a major change. We must begin to total our resources because we will find that the labour force growth is slowing down while at the same time there are increasing shortages in key sectors of the economy.
July 6, 1981

While the supply of the labour market is changing, the demand is also changing. While service work-work in the areas of public administration, clerical, management, health services, education and others-was the major stimulus for growth in the last two decades, it will increasingly decline as a supplier of jobs in Canada. We will find the slack taken up in the areas of manufacturing and resource trades, which will necessitate a very different set of requirements for skilled workers. Therefore, the emphasis will be on an area which has really been neglected for a long time. There will have to be improvement in our blue collar trades, our higher-skilled trades and our technology trades. We will have to reallocate our resources, our interest and our attention to supplying those skills. That will mean some major changes in many of the vested interests of our society, many of the educational institutions, our apprenticeship programs and many of our industrial programs. It is for this reason that we have brought in these changes to the Adult Occupational Training Act at this time, so that we are able to get a leg up to take some lead initiating those changes.

Mr. Speaker, the federal government must play a major role in helping both workers and employers to adjust to the realities of the present labour market. We must promote the integration of women, native people and disadvantaged workers into a larger field of employment. We must train more workers in skilled trades and occupations. We must help the workers already on the labour market to learn new skills without undue difficulties. I believe that we must now amend the Adult Occupational Training Act and that this will be a first step towards adapting our employment and training policies to the labour market of the 1980s.

That is from western Canada, Mr. Speaker!
Of course, we recognize the need to look at the report that will be presented shortly, we hope, by the special parliamentary committee that was established last year to examine employment opportunities in this country. We await with great interest the finding in that report as well as the report which I hope to be able to table in this House within a matter of days. Those will give us the larger picture of the entire labour market situation in Canada for the 1980s.
1 hope that the parliamentary committee report and that report from my department will open up a very far-ranging debate and consultation in the entire area of job training, job creation and employment opportunities for this country as we proceed into this new decade.
1 do not think that we can wait for the full deliberations or consultations that will be based on those reports, however. Important as they are and critical as they will be to the major transformations in our policies, we must act now. We cannot afford to lose a day or a week or a year which might impede or
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2 restrain the development of new approaches to training. Some hon. members have asked me for the assurance that passage of this legislation will not close the door to further changes in training legislation after the studies have been considered. I am pleased to offer those assurances. As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, the amendments introduced in debate on second reading are simply the prelude to a much wider range of changes that must take place.
The changes introduced tonight are necessary in order to respond to the very well defined and articulated need expressed to me by employers, by trade unions and by provincial governments. I feel it is important to have the House adopt these measures before we leave so that we can put some of the more obvious changes and innovations in our training programs in place by next fall. That would mean that we would not lose time. There is a critical time gap that we must overcome if we are to meet the shortage of skilled workers in Canada.
None of the changes proposed in this bill will in any way pre-empt the work of the parliamentary task force or the other proposals that we will be debating and consulting upon over the next several months. They will have the desired flexibility, efficiency and effectiveness that will give us a good start.
The bill we are studying today has three basic goals. The first is to simplify the administration of the Adult Occupational Training Act and to eliminate much of the unnecessary paper work that small businessmen in particular must face in developing industrial training on the shop floor.
Second, we want to make the act more flexible so that it will respond to the variety of needs in the training area.
These two sets of proposals were presented in the previous Parliament. The third set is in addition to those. It is based upon the measures introduced last January as part of the industrial assistance program which was designed to deal with communities facing industrial dislocation. The amendments to this act are an essential ingredient to enable us to fully perform all the services to those designated communities under the industrial assistance program.
As far as the specifics of this bill are concerned, I am sure we would all agree that the critical place where training must occur is in the private arena. We must provide as much encouragement and incentive to the private employer to develop on-the-job training as soon as possible.
It is my intention, through these amendments, to make the program more effective and attractive by reducing the paper work burden on employers. For this reason, one of the amendments provides a flat-rate method of reimbursing training costs. This will free employers from keeping detailed records of training expenses. When the payment for each contract can be based on a composite, single rate, a great deal of time and money will be saved. The small employer will not need a legion of accountants or clerical workers to keep records on each worker in the training program but will be able to apply for a training agreement with the department under a flat rate formula.

July 6, 1981
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
The amendment has particular appeal for the small employer, the employer who provides the majority of jobs in this country but until now has not provided a great deal of training. Through this amendment, we hope to provide further incentives to the small businessman and employer in Canada to give on-the-job training.
Employers will also benefit from the change which will allow us to help with the cost of training that is conducted outside Canada. I want to caution hon. members that we would use this particular provision very sparingly. I believe we must develop and enhance our own training facilities, but there are certain skills that can only be acquired abroad. By way of example, Mr. Speaker, just last week I received a letter from the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) who sits on the opposition benches. Ele indicated that one of the oil companies in his city wanted to send six trainees to a program in Houston to develop a specialized skill for the oil industry that is only available in that city. As the act now stands, unfortunately I could not provide direct assistance to that employer for the training program. If the House were so kind as to allow quick passage of this bill, then we would be able to respond quickly to the very fervent appeal of the hon. member for Calgary West. Six new trainees would soon arrive in the wonderful city of Houston to be trained in these new skills.
There are skills that cannot be obtained in this country, Mr. Speaker, and so we need to provide the opportunity for workers to go abroad. We think we can provide support to the private small employer by giving some assistance under the training act to enable that to take place.
One of the most important amendments in this bill extends the period in which we will allow support for training beyond the 52 weeks now contained in the act. We have recognized that as we move into a high technology economy, we must develop high-skill trades. In many instances those skills cannot be acquired within the 52-week period allowed in the present act.
Hon. members know that much of our effort in the past has been concentrated on short-term job entry skills. Now, because of changing economic conditions, we must shift to occupations which require a longer training such as tool and die makers, sheet metal workers, industrial mechanics and machinists. All of these require more than 52 weeks of training.
Again I can speak, by way of example, of a representation made to me two or three weeks ago in the province of Saskatchewan. The native organizations in that province had developed programs of training and management skills for native people so that they could go back to band councils and non-profit corporations and develop management aptitudes to make those programs work. At the present time we cannot provide training beyond the 52-week period. This is another very important program that could go ahead if we could allow the additional time that is required for training. We would use this authority with a great deal of care and caution and obviously would consult with the provinces regarding the credentials and standards required. We would be able to provide for the additional training beyond the 52 weeks. This
would give an incentive to people to develop high-skill trades in Canada.

Another important and complementary amendment would erase the present requirement that people in need of skill training wait one year after leaving high school before they can be referred to institutional training. The amendment would allow a person to go from a high school program directly into an institutional training program. This would give an opportunity to young people in particular, to move directly into high-skill programs. In this context, I want to mention the representation of the hon. member for York South-Weston (Mrs. Appolloni). The hon. member indicated that perhaps in the next round of amendments we might even consider waiving the rule for those who have not yet reached the high school leaving age but who do want to enter the high school trades. I think it is a useful proposal to consider. 1 am attracted to it and I would welcome further representation. But again it comes back to the basic point that we are not interested here in paper credentials; we are interested in getting people trained. Therefore, we want to eliminate some of the overregulation and some of the kinds of difficulties and handicaps that have been put in the way of people getting access immediately to training programs.
A further important amendment in this area, and one that I personally believe would make a major improvement in our training capacity in Canada, is that this bill, with these amendments, would provide authority to negotiate industrial training contracts with persons or groups other than employers. This will give us the flexibility to make use of additional training expertise or resources.
Up to this time we have been limited either to institutional training places provided by provincial governments or to individual employers or groups of employers. Under this amendment, again subject to provincial standards or rules to make sure that the quality of training is high, we would be able to negotiate with trade unions to provide a training program for their membership. We could negotiate with agencies, such as the non-profit organizations like an Indian organization or a social agency which had the capacity or competence to provide specialized training in those areas.
Again, one of the areas in which we have been conducting much negotiation over the past several months has been with native groups to develop native-based institutions to supply workers for the big megaprojects in western Canada. Our experience demonstrates that through such institutions as the Blue Quill school in Alberta and the Indian training institute in Saskatchewan, natives can provide first-class training for their own resources. This amendment would give us the ability to provide a much broader range of sources of training for
July 6, 1981

Canadians. Therefore, it would give us a multiplication of opportunities and a multiplication of resources.
Here we come back to the issue of flexibility to give us a broader range and more effective response in the training area. Bill C-67 is aimed not only at making our training programs more effective and flexible, it is also aimed at increasing the financial flexibility under the program. Employers are now reimbursed for their trainees' wages at a rate which must not exceed the maximum training allowance set for people enrolled in courses at provincial training institutions. In the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, and indeed in other areas of the country such as British Columbia where wages are rapidly increasing, the maximum allowable weekly payment for trainees under the existing act is simply not enough. The bill would give us the ability to increase this payment and aid employers in these high-wages regions who may have to pay more than $500 a week to attract potential trainees.
I have also referred to the changing labour market conditions of the 1980s because it is important to realize the kind of challenges and demands that we will face. One of the most critical challenges to which this government has already devoted a high degree of attention is coping with the impact of sweeping technological change. This will be of particular interest to members from Ontario and Quebec, where major technology adjustments are taking place in some key traditional industries. In line with this thinking, the third goal of the proposed amendments is to enable designated workers and communities to deal more effectively with the consequences of industrial disruption.
We introduced the special industrial adjustment program last January. Within that program are a number of labour adjustment programs: portable wages, assistance for early retirement and employment incentives. The amendments proposed in Bill C-67 will further strengthen our ability to deal with workers in those communities that are affected by industrial change, such as the automobile industry, the textile industry and the shipbuilding industry. They will encourage workers to learn new skills by permitting us to offer training allowances at a period when workers are laid off in these designated industries. One of the unfortunate consequences in an economic downturn is that apprentices and trainees are usually the first fired because of seniority rules and other kinds of regulations which have grown up and evolved over the years. The first people who are the victims of industrial change are those, in many ways, who should be the last victims. I am referring to those who provide the new skills for the future. Under these amendments we will enable the trainee to go to either a new institution to continue his training or to provide for an additional allowance for that company to allow the trainee to stay on the job. Therefore, we will be able to smooth out the up and down cycles of the economic pattern so that it will not drastically affect the training opportunities of many of our workers. That is of critical importance in many of our higher industrialized provinces and regions which, by shifting the burden of the economic downturn on to apprentices or trainees, gives short shrift for the future. People who are being
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
laid off now are the future skilled technicians, technologists and manual workers whom we will need two or three years down the line in order to maintain our economic growth.
In view of that particular serious need, the amendments we propose in this second reading are of great importance. They add to the impetus and necessity for us to put these programs into place as part of our industrial adjustment system so we can provide the incentives and supports, encourage workers to train for those occupations in demand, to leave occupations where work is obsolescent and to move into new occupations where the work is to be found.
The incentive allowance contained within these amendments would give workers up to 70 per cent of their previous earnings, with a weekly ceiling of $220 per week.
Bill C-67 is one, I believe, on which all members of this House can agree. I do not believe that the training of workers in Canada is an issue which lends itself to rigorous partisan division. There can certainly be different points of view as to the kinds of amendments that can be made, improvements, but I repeat, this is just the beginning of a substantially wholesale change in the wide arena of training opportunities which Canadians will have to debate and discuss over the months and the years ahead.
Bill C-67 gives us immediate tools and instruments to apply at a time when we see the gap for workers getting shorter. Unless we start now and begin to overcome that gap, years hence members of this Parliament will be looking back with some degree of regret that this session of Parliament did not act in an expeditious way to pass this bill.
The improvements contained in Bill C-67 should recommend themselves to all members of the House. Because we must act quickly and with dispatch, I trust and hope that it will be possible to secure the consent of members of this House for a speedy passage of this bill so it can become law this summer and we can get on with the new training horizons that we must face by this fall.

Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to take part in the debate on Bill C-67, an act to amend the Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2. This act proposes amendments to an act which, I think we all agree, needs updating badly.
We on this side are concerned that the minister is making changes that do not fit exactly the recommendation of Parliament's select Committee on Employment Opportunities for the '80s. I am a member of that committee. I must say that in the last year I have enjoyed my work immensely. I know that several members of the committee wish to speak on this bill as well as other members of my party.
Something I find rather amusing is that everyone on the other side is in a hurry. We get to July and they want to rush everything through. This minister is no exception. He said we need to rush this through, we need it in a hurry, these programs cannot go on without legislation. 1 am surprised to

Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2 hear that coming from him because not having the legislative authority to do it has never before stopped the government from doing something.

speechtext:
I do not have time to name them all. The government introduces bills at the last minute and then wants to rush them through the House so that it can get away for the summer. However, this is a very important subject and it must be discussed thoroughly.
In this country we have a very serious problem. We have a shortage of skilled workers and a shortage in certain professions. We have about one million unemployed. According to the latest statistics, the unemployment rate across Canada is
7.1	per cent. The goverment likes to talk about that figure in glowing terms. Even the Governor of the Bank of Canada is now in on the act. His definition of full employment is 7 per cent. I am not an economist, but even I know that is not realistic. I doubt whether there are many people in this House who believe this is a realistic figure.
The government and the minister failed to mention that for young persons under the age of 24, unemployment is in the 12.7 per cent range; well over 13 per cent for men that age and under 12 per cent for women. This group makes up 25 per cent of the age 15 and over population, but accounts for 45 per cent of the unemployed.
In the last 14 years the unemployment rate for young people has dropped in only 5 years, but over that period the rate of unemployment for youth has risen from 5.6 to 12.7 per cent, the present rate. Their share of unemployment has risen from 40 per cent to 47 per cent in that time. Of the close to one half million young people unemployed, 50 per cent have less than a grade 10 education.
The problem is immense, as we have found out over the past year when studying and debating the situation in Canada. Recommendations will be forthcoming from the employment opportunities committee. I urge the minister to pay heed to what the committee recommends. I can assure him and his predecessors that we will not rest until the report is implemented or reasons given which prove conclusively that it would be impossible to implement. I am sure pressure will come from all sides of this House.
There are many shortages in some regions of Canada and a surplus of manpower in others. Bringing the two together is a major problem that must be addressed. Are our young people getting the proper training? Why have we not trained in Canada? Is training going on now?
I think it is fair to say that the training going on in Canada is generally of good quality. There are some areas where the equipment being used with which to teach is outdated and some instructors have not had an opportunity to upgrade themselves in the latest techniques, but generally there is good training.
Most definitely there is not enough training being carried out in Canada. One may wonder why. Traditionally, Canada has imported its skilled labour from many countries of the world. It was easy to find the tool and die makers, the aeronautical technologists, the machine operators, and one could go on and on. However, that supply is fast disappearing for a number of reasons.
First, this government changed its emphasis regarding immigrants from one of importing necessary skills to family reunification. I am all for family reunification. As the minister knows, 1 am probably knocking on his door as often as any member of this House regarding those people who immigrate to Canada and make a new start here. However, one statistic which concerns me about our immigration policy at present is that only 24 per cent of those immigrating to Canada have the skills that are required. If the trend we have experienced over the last few years since the act was changed and came into effect in April 1978 continues, the number will be down to 12 per cent in two years. That is dangerous.
The second reason, and this may be hard for some Canadians to understand, is that there are not as many skilled people anxious to make a new start in Canada as has been the experience in the past. With Canada's slip from second to seventh place in standard of living, we are not quite as attractive as we might have been in the past.
The third reason, and this is becoming more of a factor every year, is that with major projects around the world, megaprojects or world projects being carried out in many countries, a shortage of skilled labour is being felt everywhere. Other countries are coming to Canada to try to entice our skilled labour to go to their country to work on major projects. Australia is a prime example of that. Of course, the falling birth rate around the world is another factor. Skilled labour is in short supply.
Canada's manufacturing and service industries must train, and must train in a very big way, if we are to remain competitive in the world marketplace. How do we go about it?
I do not want to second guess the findings of the committee, but I think I can sum up our recommendations by saying we need co-operation, we need emphasis in certain areas of our country, but we have the capacity in Canada to do the job.
Let me discuss co-operation for just a moment. The Dominion of Canada has two levels of government which share certain responsibilities. Therefore, it is important that there be co-operation between the federal and provincial levels. I am very concerned that the back of the spirit of co-operation may be broken and positive moves will be required to heal that broken back. The controversy over the Constitution and the controversy over energy prices have poisoned the atmoshpere.
I am sad to say that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) has not seen fit to have a meeting with the provincial ministers responsible for education, manpower and apprenticeship programs and the federal government with regard to its involvement in manpower planning and training. Yes, he made a flying trip across Canada when he was first appointed some 16 or 17 months ago, but
July 6, 1981

since then he has not had meetings, and the two levels are unmistakably entwined. As recently as June 8, 1981 ministers responsible for manpower in four western provinces and the Yukon and Northwest Territories met and set up advisory teams which will address common labour market issues in western Canada, issues such as manpower training, manpower planning and analysis, including mobility of labour, and the effects of immigration. They stated that they would ask to meet the federal Minister of Employment and Immigration to discuss changes prior to implementation. In their communique the participants stated the following:
We hope this kind of consultation is an example the federal government will follow in future and thereby remove one of the issues-that of federal intrusion, unilaterally and without consultation, into fields of education and training, which are under provincial and territorial government jurisdiction.
That is quite an indictment. The situation must change and, being such an open individual, I am sure the minister will take the advice of that committee and its report in this regard and hopefully will call meetings of manpower ministers from across this fair land, and not just the western ministers.
There must be co-operation between labour and management. As I mentioned before and as the minister mentioned in his remarks, more must be done about job training in order to keep Canada competitive. The fault lies at many levels. No one person is to blame for the lack of manpower training in this country. One of those levels is union and management. Unions naturally want to protect those who are working, the journeymen. That is understandable, but unions must realize that to provide a trained work force a number of apprentices must be assured that they will finish their training from start to finish. This can be negotiated and put into contacts.
I toured Orenda Engines in Mississauga. I wish the minister would take time sometime to go down there are take a look at that company. The average age of its skilled workers frightens me. Its skilled work force is aging rapidly and approaching retirement, and there is not one apprentice in the place. This is in the aeronautics industry, in which we all know Canada has a great future. What will happen to companies like this five to ten years down the road? They will be knocking at the minister's door and saying, "We want a mission to Britain to bring some skilled workers from their aeronautic industry back to Canada to work here." They are not training.
We visited Germany and Britain as part of our study, and one of the things we found was that when an apprentice takes on an apprenticeship, he finishes it. He is assured of finishing it. He is not assured of a job, but he is assured of his training, much like our young people going to university. They are guaranteed to finish their courses and to get their degrees. The same is true in our community colleges. Apprenticeships in Canada are not like that. They are last on, first off, and that has to change to assure apprentices that they will complete their education. In Germany 80 per cent to 90 per cent of the companies train skilled workers. In England, it is between 70 per cent and 75 per cent. In Canada it is 20 per cent. We have a critical shortage, and the minister now sees fit to bring in a
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
piecemeal bill. It will help somewhat-I do not argue about that at all-but in no way does it have the answer to Canada's manpower problems.
One of the other problems is mobility of labour. There tends to be a double standard on the gouvernment side. Case after case has been raised. The Department of Employment and Immigration is not allowing a constituent of mine to apply for a job in the metropolitan area of Toronto because he happens to live 100 yards outside an arbitrary boundary set up by personnel. The only reason it was set up was to weed out applications. It was a method of weeding out applications. To my way of thinking, that is not mobility of labour. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) is here tonight. He should be ashamed. Secretaries can apply for work in his department only if they live in Ontario and Quebec. That is some mobility of labour! Pilots for the government must come from one province, or they cannot apply. There is no mobility of labour there. We see this type of thing happening in the government, and we hear great pious remarks from hon. members opposite about how they have to solve the mobility of labour problem, but I suggest they take a look at their own closets before they ask other people to clean up their closets.
We begin to understand why a premier of a province, such as Premier Peckford, says, "Jobs for my people first, and then we will go much wider." Some of my friends opposite from Quebec have discussed the problem with me. Naturally they want jobs created in the province of Quebec for Quebecers first. I understand that, but the double standards which are being preached are very unfair.
Then there are special interest groups of workers with limited access to the labour market. Discrimination is a barrier to access. In the labour market there is a distinction which is made based solely on race, sex, age or physical handicaps. In the case of natives, they suffer general discrimination on the part of employers. This is particularly visible in the service sector where the jobs require contact with the public. In many cases this discrimination takes place during the selection of candidates, while in other cases it takes place during employment. This situation pushes natives to choose social welfare rather than being subjected to such humiliations. Other groups make much less frequent use of the word "discrimination", which leads to the belief that barriers are less insurmountable or the work environment less hostile.
However, women claim to be subject to job discrimination and discrimination in training possibilities. The same happens to physically handicapped persons and to senior workers. Natives face problems which seem deeper than those of other groups. Natives want to have jobs, as do all citizens of Canada. They find the working environment alienating because it is insufficiently flexible to their socio-cultural peculiarities. It is therefore necessary to establish improved dialogue between the world of business and industry on the one hand and natives on the other. I feel that the attitudes of employers must change, and concrete measures should be taken in this regard. Unemployment among natives is alarming. Unemployment rates

July 6, 1981
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
reaching up to 90 per cent in some areas are quoted. This problem will only become more pressing as a massive influx of young natives into the labour market is forecast over the next ten years. Given that the current employment possibilities on the reserves are limited, these young people will increase the ranks of the urban unemployed, and they must be trained.
Women also have specific problems to overcome in order to enter the labour market and to keep stable employment. They are often limited to subordinate, low-paying jobs. They have no hope of moving out of them by orienting themselves toward non-traditional types of female employment because of rigid social attitudes which classify them by sexist stereotypes.
Labour market structures are another important barrier, particularly for those women who have family responsibilities. The rigidity of work schedules is a case in point. So is the limited availability of part-time jobs, shared employment and so on. The other main obstacle to the access of women to the labour market is the absence of employment support services. Representatives of women's groups agree that employment prospects will remain limited as long as there are no day care services easily accessible to all. It is also necessary to introduce other improvements such as better professional counselling, which, I might add, is handled very capably in Outreach programs. In summary, if it is desired that the work of women contribute to economic performance, it is necessary to introduce services to facilitate their access to the labour market.
The physically handicapped, Mr. Speaker, even in this year of the handicapped are still perceived as being incapable of making a positive social contribution. If their access to work were facilitated and if changes in the social attitude towards them could be introduced, they could become productive. The current rate of unemployment among young people is high, due no doubt to demographic factors, career choice errors and, at least partly, to the imposition of abusive entry requirements for jobs, as well as demands for previous experience which is often not necessary. The attitudes of unions, for example the closed shop, would also limit their employment opportunities. These are people who really do need help and training in a manpower planning program, and this is not specifically addressed in Bill C-67. As the minister knows full well, the matter must be addressed and quickly.
The matter of financing of professional training is an age old problem. Who should finance the training? How can the present financing system be improved? I personally feel manpower training is as important a part of post-secondary education as is university or community college education. Manpower on the job training, apprenticeship training and skills training in technical fields are a part of our post-secondary education system and should be treated as such. I think the financing system can be grouped under four main themes: Financing problems which enterprises must face; current policy on grants and the means to improve it; use of the fiscal
system as a means to subsidize training; the establishment of a grant levy system.
Training involves costs for firms either directly or indirectly by an increase in the cost of production. Although these costs may eventually be recovered in the shape of higher productivity and eventual reduction of bottlenecks if the employee turnover rate is low, there is still an immediate burden the firm must bear. Small and medium-sized businesses are often unable to bear these costs and need some kind of assistance. In this regard, in spite of an often questionable allocation of funds, government assistance for training is very important to those firms. In spite of this assistance, a large share is borne by the firm. In certain sectors the share would be in the order of 75 to 80 per cent, and even more. Under these circumstances it is not surprising to find that the training activity is lower than what the companies themselves would like to maintain. Therefore, they should receive greater government assistance in the form of wage subsidies, capital subsidies for the equipment required for training, and general subsidies for human resources they allocate to training. Otherwise they cannot have a sufficient level of activity in these fields, particularly at a time when profit margins are low, non-existent or negative.
In their judgment, government assistance is further justified because they finance through corporate income taxes an education system which supplies at no cost trained personnel to other sectors, particularly the service sector.
As to the present grant policy, we have heard that the desirability of maintaining this policy is not uniform. One group, mainly business representatives, wish to maintain the principle. As for changes in fund allocation, it would be desirable that government offer financial assistance for training periods of up to four years. In addition, the assistance offered for the training of apprentices should cover a greater share, or even all, of the costs incurred by the firm. There is also a general feeling that training should more closely match the needs of the local community and this should lead to different financing mechanisms. Funds should be redistributed to support initiatives at the local level. This is being done in some areas to a limited degree. Other groups, mainly labour representatives, would like the government to withdraw completely from the financing of training programs, or at least play only a complementary or ancillary role. The reason invoked is that training is usually the responsibility of the firm and it must therefore fully assume it. Many raise the issue, however, from the viewpoint of economic efficiency. Such a system of complete self-financing has the advantage of assuring society that the cost to the firm of trained personnel more closely approaches its real economic cost. Furthermore, the parties directly involved are better equipped to define the over-all needs for financing and to undertake an efficient allocation of resources to training.
Some people suggest the use of the fiscal system to expand training and distribute its benefits and costs in a more equitable way. There are already employment tax credit programs, and it is felt that they have had a positive effect on training. Some people have proposed innovations. For example, grants
July 6, 1981

could be given to training in the form of corporate tax credits, or tax breaks could be given to those who must train highly qualified manpower, or the training costs should be made tax deductible. Alternatively, a special tax could be imposed on business enterprises which use journeymen, while allowing these firms to deduct the total training expenses from their taxable income. All these ideas have been presented to the Standing Committee on Employment Opportunities for the '80s.
Then, Mr. Speaker, there is the grant levy system. This has been discussed a great deal by the committee. The reactions vary from very supportive to very unfavourable, with a wide range of opinions between the two. I am sure my colleague from the NDP will be touching on this a little later on. The main thrust of the argument of those who support this type of financing is that it distributes training expenses for a sector equitably among the firms, thereby eliminating piracy from one business to another. It would guarantee firms that their training costs will be reimbursed and penalize those which do not train people. It is therefore seen as a way of eliminating the free-riders and increasing the efficiency and volume of training. For those who express opposition, there are different reasons behind the positions they take. The system is inefficient, it would only lead to compounding of the existing problems, or it is inequitable as it does not treat all sectors equally and penalize the goods-producing sector while imposing no additional costs on the service sector.
Positions between the two extremes provide a more qualified argumentation. Witnesses in this group recognize as a whole that at least part of the training costs must be transferred to industry and that industry must make a concerted effort to increase training. Three aspects of the grant-levy system caused some reticence. The need to apply such a system to all industrial sectors has not been demonstrated. Some sectors could establish their own self-financing system for training- and it was indicated that this is now the case in some industries-without being forced to do so and without having to create a new bureaucratic structure. If the government were to establish the system, it was felt that it should be on a very limited basis or through pilot projects.
Before formulating recommendations, the central question to be solved is to know whether or not firms need government assistance for training. The following recommendations are presented in three groups: recommendations which support the position, first, of those who believe that government financial assistance must be increased, second, of those who believe that such assistance must be abolished, and third of those who have mixed positions on the matter. Increased government assistance to firms, particularly those of small and medium size which have difficulty in meeting the high cost of training, must be maintained. Training assistance must be increased. Government should consider expanding this assistance into the area of capital grants for the equipment required for training, as well as to the wages and subsidies for employers who are doing the training. Government should proceed to reallocate funds cur-
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
rently earmarked for training so as to link them to initiatives taken at the local level. In other words, the government should target its expenditures more carefully.
Then there are those who would eliminate government assistance to the firms. The government should recognize that training is the responsibility of the firm and withdraw completely from the field. It should redirect funds currently assigned to training programs toward training fields centred on the third sector of the economy. Other positions somewhere in between suggest that the government should use the taxation system to encourage firms to become involved in training. I see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans) sitting over there thinking about that one. To this end the government should provide tax credits for training. Perhaps it should even increase them. The government should make all training costs tax deductible, or it should introduce a special tax for enterprises which use trained labour and combine this measure with the tax deductibility of training costs.
Those are some of the problems and some of the solutions which were presented to the Standing Committee on Employment Opportunities for the '80s. We should think about some of these solutions very carefully before forthcoming recommendations are made. This is why we are somewhat concerned that the minister is presenting the bill before the recommendations from the committee are presented to him.
Bill C-67 provides assistance in much needed areas. I am pleased the government will contract with independent groups at private educational facilities which provide excellent service. This will help us train some of the skilled workers we are missing. As I understand it, it affords the right of unions to sign intertraining contracts and to be given allowances. I am pleased with the lifting of the one-year ceiling and the revocation of the requirement that trainees must be out of school at least one year. There are many other factors in the bill with which we are very pleased. However, although we feel it is premature, we will not prevent its passage.
I should like to sum up what we feel must happen in manpower training and planning in the country. We have not seen too much evidence of it, but we assume that in this decade there will be economic policies to create growth based on the perception of long-term economic strengths which can be exploited. There is a critical skill shortage. We will not be able to achieve our growth potential without a significant investment in training. I hope the government is aware of the crisis situation.
There is a great deal of growth potential in many areas of Canada. In the east there are the energy finds with which we are all so pleased. In the west there are the megaprojects of the not too distant future. Of course there are great opportunities in more sparsely populated parts of the north. But the growth will not be achieved unless there is some significant movement in the labour force. A portion of our population will have to move to where the jobs are. Solutions will be arrived at in direct proportion to the degree to which the federal and provincial governments, as well as industry and labour groups, are willing to work together as partners in solving the prob-

Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2 lems. The solutions will have to encompass a strong sense of the uniqueness of particular communities, industries, cultural groups, regions and required skills.
This bill does not make a dint on the problem. The recommendations are fine but they are piecemeal. It really does not take a fresh, imaginative, gutsy approach to the problem. In typical Grit fashion, throw a little money at it; put a band-aid here and a tourniquet there; patch up the holes and make it look good, as if we were doing something-"Public, here we are; we are great and we are helping you out."
Could it be that this stop-gap measure is put in so that the government can wait for the little munchkin from the office of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), The Alberta boy who cannot win a seat in that province for the Liberals and must be parachuted into Spadina? Is the government awaiting him? I notice one of his priorities is manpower planning. Perhaps that is why the government has not brought in a comprehensive bill and is not looking at the problem in total. Perhaps the government is parachuting this Alberta boy into Spadina because it knows he cannot win out west and that he will take the place of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) in planning. I would advise the minister to watch himself.

We of the Progressive Conservative party are dedicated to long-term meaningful employment for all residents of Canada. We will work hard toward that end. In the meantime we must put up with this "stick your finger in the dike" approach to solving what is a crisis problem in Canada. I wish the minister would wait for the report of the Standing Committee on Employment Opportunities for the '80s, the Dodge report and the other reports which are reaching fruition at the present time. He should take time to absorb them and then bring in comprehensive, exciting, imaginative, workable solutions to the manpower crisis in Canada.

subtopic: ADULT OCCUPATIONAL TRAINING ACT, NO. 2 MEASURETO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for almost a year now a parliamentary committee on employment, representative of the three political parties in Parliament, has been meeting. The committee held hearings from one end of the country to the other. It heard submissions from industry, labour, educators, community groups, outreach organizations, native organizations and handicapped people. All of these groups were extemely critical of government manpower employment training programs until now. They were especially critical of the federal Department of Employment and immigration. All of them expressed the view that we needed to have a great deal more on the job training than we have had.
When the committee visited a number of countries in Europe, it was able to see how backward Canada was as
compared to the western European countries in terms of training people to fill the skilled jobs which every modern industrialized country needs. Virtually all the representations we heard stressed the need to have a great deal more decentralization of the planning and the administration of programs than we have had in the past. All of them believe-and this was particularly true of both employer and employee groups, union groups-that no programs could succeed unless there were the fullest consultation between labour, management, educators and governments at the federal and provincial levels. When it is ready, the committee will be tabling a report which, I suppose, 97 per cent of the members support. I am amazed at how few of the views which the committee heard and the opinions which the committee formed are embodied in the bill before us or in the statement made by the minister tonight, or even on earlier occasions since he became the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy).
Before going into some of the difficulties I see in the bill I would like to spend a few minutes making it clear that as far as our party is concerned we believe it is impossible to plan and implement a really successful job creation and training program which will be of any real benefit, unless we are committed to a program of full employment. If we do not have full employment, all we will accomplish will be a better educated and better trained group of unemployed.
Back in 1945 a Liberal government tabled a white paper on employment and income in which a policy of full employment was laid down on behalf of that government. The white paper expressed the belief of the government that a job should be provided for every Canadian who wished to work and the adoption of policies which would achieve that end.

Members opposite shout their agreement and I agree with them.
In the first annual review of the Economic Council in 1964, full employment was discussed. The council estimated that full employment in Canada would be reached when we had an unemployment rate of 3 per cent. It is interesting to note that in the periods after these goals were affirmed, they were substantially met. Between 1946 and 1953 the unemployment rate averaged 3 per cent. After the review of the Economic Council in the mid-sixties, to which I have referred, we had three full employment years between 1965 and 1967 when the unemployment rate averaged 3.8 per cent. Since that time, the unemployment rate has moved steadily upward, and by the mid-1970s the average rate had almost doubled. Between 1975 and 1977 it stood at 7.4 per cent. We have now had 60 months-five years-in which the official seasonally adjusted level of unemployment has been in excess of 7 per cent. That is more than twice what the Economic Council projected back in 1963.
I would ask you to keep in mind, Mr. Speaker, that the 7 per cent rate very substantially underestimated the real rate of unemployment, since we have somewhere between 250,000 and 350,000 people who are not calculated into the official

Also accounted for in these figures are native people living on reserves. It is important to note that youth unemployment is almost twice the official rate of over 7 per cent. It is over 12 per cent. subtopic: ADULT OCCUPATIONAL TRAINING ACT, NO. 2 MEASURETO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only spoken for a few minutes. I intend to get to the guts of the bill very shortly.
As I said a moment ago, it seems to us quite fruitless to be discussing occupational training unless we really have a full employment policy. Thus, I would like to conclude this part of my speech by pointing out that over the years the government has moved away from a full employment policy, which meant 3 per cent or 4 per cent unemployment some years ago. The government now seems prepared, as does the Governor of the Bank of Canada, to accept an unemployment rate of over 7 per cent as being full employment. Our party does not accept that. We say that if that is the government's view then, in fact, the whole program of training people will be a failure.
1 would now like to deal with some of the clauses of the bill which is before us, a few of which we think move in the right direction and one or two of which we think are fundamentally wrong and which will lead to the failure of the whole program as enunciated by the minister.
Clause 1 of the bill amends the existing act to provide for training courses for periods longer than a year. That is to say, training allowances will be paid to people for more than a year who attend courses which have been approved by the department. This is a very late acceptance of a criticism which has been made in this House and outside it almost since the time the bill was first introduced. It was obvious from the beginning that, particularly for highly-skilled occupations, a one-year training course was not sufficient and, therefore, the government should have arranged for people to receive training allowances for more than a year. Hence, we greet this amendment with approval.
However, we note that this change applies only to full-time training, which we think is a mistake. We think the bill should be much more flexible. We believe that the bill should provide that part-time training courses be made available for more than a year if that is deemed to be useful to the community. This bill has an amendment which removes the former regula-
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
tion that a person would have to be out of school for a year prior to being committed to take a training course and to have training allowances. That is another provision which we have criticized for a number of years; and to the extent that it changes that and gives the government and the individuals some flexibility, we support it.
I want to spend a little time on the section which I think is extremely important and is extremely bad. The minister will not be surprised if I raise this matter because I have raised it on a number of occasions in the last few months. I refer to the section of the bill which says the following:
The commission may enter into a contract with
(a)	any employer that operates or undertakes to operate an occupational
training course . . .
(b)	any employer that arranges or undertakes to arrange for the training of
adults employed by the employer ...
(c)	any group or association of employers referred to in paragraph (a) or (b).
If there is one message which the Committee on Employment for the '80s got from almost everyone who made representations to the task force, it was that training programs would be a failure unless they were worked out in consultation with employers, with employees and with the educational institutions and the federal-provincial governments concerned. Yet here we have in this bill again the insistence of the minister and the department that the agreements worked out by the department need only be worked out with the employer or groups of employee associations.
In the last year, we have had a number of agreements announced by the minister. We had the industrial labour restructuring program, for which $350 million was provided in the budget by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). That program was to be used to help train people in part in areas like Windsor, Sept-Iles, Sydney and several other cities. Then we have had the individual agreements announced almost every week by this minister or other ministers, and I will just name some of the industries they cover: the foundry industry, the aerospace industry, the coal association, the mining association, the shipbuilding industry and the clothing and textile industry.
As I said, if there was one message which was given to the task force, it was that these programs would not succeed unless they were worked out in co-operation with both labour and management.
The committee was not the only group which got that message. I have before me a report by the major projects task force on major capital projects in Canada to the year 1980, a joint industry-labour committee set up through the good offices of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray). What does it say about employment and manpower? Let me quote, beginning on page 55 of the report. It reads:
There should be a shift in emphasis in training programs towards increased on-the-job training.

July 6, 1981
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
The minister is moving in that direction, although I think much too slowly, in these agreements, some of which I have listed. Then it goes to say:
This should involve a reallocation of spending priorities for government training programs such as the Canada Manpower Training Program.
Action will also be required to ensure the expansion of on-the-job training by industry. It is proposed that a levy-grant system be introduced on an experimental and selective, sectoral basis to impose a payroll training tax levy on employers in those industries where training-related shortages are known to exist.
I do not intend to go into detail about the levy-grant system tonight, but it recommends as follows:
Academic institutions, industry and organized labour must work together more closely to help ensure the relevancy of academic programs.
There is nothing in this bill, and there was nothing in any of the agreements announced by this minister or the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. De Bane) in their announcement about the training programs for the textile and clothing industry which would indicate that the government paid any attention to the views of labour at all. 1 raised this matter on a number of occasions, and each time the minister has brushed off the suggestions which I made. The minister knows that I was not just talking for the sake of talking, because I have here a letter sent to the minister by the national director of the United Steelworkers of America, one of the largest unions in this country. The letter is dated June 1, 1981. He deals very specifically and critically with the minister in respect to the matter which 1 am raising at the present time. Let me just quote the following sentences from the letter which the national director of the United Steelworkers of America, Gerard Docquier, sent to the minister on June 1, 1981:
The labour movement has not been consulted in the preparation of these programs.
He is talking about the coal and mining training proposals. Then he goes on to say:
Only after the fact, that is only after the programs have been announced, has there been any effort by your government to consult with the labour movement.
Then he goes on to say:
These agreements were signed on April 14 and 15 respectively and we heard about them for the first time when they were publicly announced. We were subsequently notified that officials of your department and of the associations were willing to hold a briefing session with officials of our union. This cannot by any means be described as consultations.
Then he goes on to say, further:
The union is, for all practical purposes, completely denied any opportunity to contribute to a program that will directly affect its members. In other words, the people who will be touched by the programs have no input into them.
Let me pause for a minute to remind the minister of one of the arguments put forward by the hon. member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) when he pointed out the difficulties which now exist when there is a slowdown in some plant, and following the usual practice, the last people hired are the first people laid off. Therefore, according to the hon. member for Brampton-Georgetown, many times apprentices who are being trained for the skilled jobs for which there is such a shortage are laid off. Is it any wonder that unions will insist on that kind of procedure? They want to protect their
members. If they are not consulted, as this letter indicates they have not been consulted by the minister in these new agreements, is it any wonder that unions will be less than enthusiastic about co-operating with the government and with employers in the programs to try to meet the skilled shortages which we are beginning to see?
Then Mr. Docquier goes on to write about that industrial labour training program, the $350 million program announced last October, and points out that the CLC wanted to be consulted on that program but it was not. Regarding that program and how it was worked out, he said:
Officials of the CLC were told of the program late on a Friday and it was made public on the following Monday. They were also told then that labour would be involved in the committees at the level of the designated communities for the implementation of the programs.
Then he goes on to say:
If labour had been consulted on the training agreements or the industrial adjustment program, it would have meant that labour would have had an opportunity to provide some input into the preparation of the programs. This has obviously not taken place and we regret it because better programs might have resulted from consultation with the people affected.
What we have now is a criticism of the programs which the minister has been announcing, as I say, almost every week. This bill enshrines in legislation the same kind of policy that is so harshly criticized by unions and is ignored by the government.

and to talk to them about their needs within the next year and to train people for those jobs.

These people had the assurance that if they succeeded and finished the course, there would be jobs for them. We were told that 75 per cent of those who graduated found jobs, and a year later 50 per cent of them were still working. We have nothing like that, Mr. Speaker. We have very few projects which train native people. In Winnipeg, Regina, Calgary or Vancouver there are large numbers of unemployed native people. They are not in the police department or the fire department in Winnipeg or in the parks department. They are not in the federal government. There are no native letter carriers or mail sorters in the Post Office. I could list 25 or 30 occupations in Winnipeg in which native people could find employment if they had the training, which they do not have, or if they had the work experience, which they do not have.
We would like to see the kind of programs begun in the United States and which have been so successful there. Nongovernmental, non-profit or even private enterprise projects train people who have not been able to find jobs, particularly the women, the handicapped, the native people, to mention just three groups. They are helped to get the training and move into jobs where they are needed. Yet we see very little of that in this bill. While there are some facets of this bill with which we can agree and make improvements over what we have had until now, we see very little if any reason to believe that the government believes enough in full employment to devise policies which will move us toward full employment. The government talks about the need for restraint rather than the necessity of job creation.
