speechtext:
I want to emphasize that in Ontario, a province which provides half the nation's output in goods, it is expected that in four years there will be a shortage of some 35,000 skilled workers. Ratio figures do, of course, vary but as a minimum this shortage will create other unskilled job losses of 175,000 positions.
In Alberta, the Alberta Oil Sands Technology and Research Authority is predicting severe shortages in a wide range of highly skilled jobs, including a shortfall of some 1,000 scientists a year.
Finally, the Minister of Employment and Immigration said in Halifax on May 27 last that Canadians might have two to three years' grace before the bubble of imbalances in the labour market bursts, causing severe shortages of skilled labour.
The burning question is how did this problem develop. Unfortunately, like most disgraceful and blameworthy situations, the culprits have no end of excuses. Government, industry, unions, secondary and post-secondary institutions, even society in general, can all be said to share the responsibility for the labour shortage problems of today. Our responsibility here is to examine the federal role, of which Bill C-67 is one response and only one, to the impending crisis.
Recently, a publication called Odyssey carried a three-part special report on the skilled labour shortage here in Canada. One comment in the third part of that report read:
Ottawa's approach to training is something of a dog's breakfast.
I considered referring to that article this evening but I ultimately decided not to do so because I find the situation reprehensible. In fact, I despair at the inability of this government and the minister to address this problem seriously.
Over and over again, Canadians and the Progressive Conservative party pounded away at this government on the issue of the Constitution, making the essential criticism that the entire process was arbitrary and authoritarian. Just as the provinces were ignored and snubbed by the government over the Constitution, so now this minister is barging ahead with his bill without a full discussion with provincial authorities or even the labour movement. To add further insult to this, the minister will not shy away from impressing upon everyone else the need for consultation and co-operation with the provinces.
Only a week ago, the minister said in Toronto that what was needed was intelligence work, a co-operative effort and a wide-ranging debate on the issues. Presumably this will take place after the passage of Bill C-67.
July 6, 1981

Once again, it falls to the Progressive Conservative party to speak out for the provinces. And who should know better than the provinces what the industries of those provinces want and need. Why would the federal government bother with committees on manpower needs if it is going to ignore the provinces on amendments to the Adult Occupational Training Act?
If we are to make any headway on the skilled labour front, and I have to join in the criticism levelled against the federal government, the federal government will have to get off its high horse and work in concert with the provinces. However, I doubt that the provinces could really object to any of the amendments proposed in Bill C-67. The simple fact is that, given the magnitude of the problem, these amendments are woefully inadequate. No one can snub a little help, but you sure can scream for more.
For example, an extra $25 a week over and above regular UIC payments is to be given to laid off workers who enter an apprenticeship training program. What, may 1 ask, is so magical about $25? How or why was this figure arrived at? On an individual basis, the amount is neither here nor there, yet for the government it represents a significant expenditure. As such, I must conclude that this is neither an incentive nor a necessary expense, and is therefore simply in keeping with the government's long-term policy of simply throwing money at a problem.
Various other amendments denote housekeeping efforts as opposed to improvements as such. The one-year ceiling on government assistance to trainees has been lifted; assistance for short-term training outside Canada is provided for, and various areas and industries are to receive increased assistance for apprenticeships. These measures are of some help but they pale by comparison with the magnitude of the problem.
In that regard, allow me to give the House an example. The General Motors plant in Windsor, Ontario will have 50 apprentice positions opening up this year. GM officials expect some 2,000 applicants. How, I hate to ask again, is Bill C-67 going to be of any help in a mess like that, where there is such a demand?
In a country like Canada which can boast of a highly educated population and a relatively high standard of living, surely we can do better than Bill C-67. We know what the problem is and we know that increased apprenticeship programs are a good part of the solution. Prior to this mail strike, I had been receiving correspondence from constituents who were truly caught in a bind, seeking an apprenticeship training program.
For these people academic upgrading is the solution as it supplies an income coupled with a comfortable atmosphere. Once their academic upgrading has been completed, they are then able to undertake training at community or technical colleges. For reasons not yet clear, Niagara College is cutting back on its very necessary adult training program.
The other avenue is apprenticeship programs, and that is where the respective governments are going to have to work in
Adult Occupational Training Act, No. 2
concert. For its part, the federal government should be doing everything it possibly can to assist and encourage people to enrol in apprenticeship programs. Bill C-67 is not going to do this. As I stated earlier, this minister and this government will have to act quickly on the skilled labour shortage problem or Canadians will be in serious trouble.
I began by saying that my riding of St. Catharines has been experiencing high unemployment for some time and that local industries were going begging for skilled labour. The amendments proposed in Bill C-67 to the Adult Occupational Training Act are not sufficiently meaningful to change that situation, nor do the amendments represent any meaningful consultation with the provincial authorities. It is therefore with regret that I cannot support this bill. It is simply too little, too late.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to put forward some views I have on a question I asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) on June 12, 1980. I took exception at that point to the reply I was given. I do not think it was adequate and at this time I would just like to read the reply the minister gave to a question I asked in which I pointed out that Alsands at Fort McMurray and the Imperial Oil Cold Lake project were in danger of being shelved and stopped. That was on June 12, 1980, over a year ago. I pointed out there would be a delay, and 1 pointed out the real cost not only to the Canadian economy but also to the small businessman in the communities of Fort McMurray, Cold Lake, Grand Centre, Bonnyville, and the surrounding areas as well as to people in Alberta generally but, more particularly, to the industrial areas of Ontario and Quebec. The minister said:
Adjournment Debate
Madam Speaker, I would only answer the hon. member by indicating that the federal government is ready to and has approved proceeding with those two plants. As a matter of fact, Petro-Canada, with Alberta Gas Trunk Line, has already come out with a proposal for another plant, a third plant. So the federal government is very supportive of the construction of more tar sand plants. The companies are ready to go ahead with those plants.
I am sure the minister did not mean to mislead the House, but that is what he most certainly did because the companies are not ready to proceed with those plants. Spokesmen for Alsands and Imperial Oil have stated emphatically, over and over again during the past year, that they will not proceed with the plants even if they have the approval of the Alberta government because a pricing regime has not been established for the production from the two megaprojects in northeastern Alberta.
I am alarmed that no one has taken these statements of the spokesmen of these companies seriously enough to approach this very critical problem. The government has established and said that it would offer to the oil sands plants, the megaprojects, a floor price of $38 per barrel and tie any further price increases to the consumer price index. The companies have stated emphatically-and I must agree with them on this point because I live in Fort McMurray and I understand what they are talking about-that the consumer price index, as it is measured across Canada, does not relate to the costs experienced in northeastern Alberta in communities such as Fort McMurray, Cold Lake, Grand Centre and Bonnyville. It does not reflect the production costs and the construction costs because of the high cost of living and the high cost of contruction experienced in those areas. All these factors add to the cost of producing the oil. It is much higher and continues to escalate much more rapidly than the consumer price index. It is based upon what could be called a construction price index or whatever, but it is there.
I feel the minister, perhaps inadvertently, misled the House when he said that Alberta Gas Trunk and Petro-Canada were ready to proceed with another plant. Certainly in committee I asked officials of Petro-Canada if they were going to proceed with the development of a tar sands plant in northeastern Alberta in the heavy oil and tar sands area. They answered emphatically that they were. I asked them when they would have the plant on construction and producing. The minimum time required was at least ten years. They said that they were ready to proceed immediately, but in fact they are not ready because it takes five years of intensive work on the site to test the site area, to test the way the bitumen lies in the sand and to test how they will mine it. It takes at least five years to do the necessary preparatory work before they can get on with the construction of the plant. So I take exception to those answers.
In the one minute remaining I should like to point out that the government is still dragging its feet on a very fundamental issue. It is obvious the government has taken the position that it will take control and be damned about a secure supply of energy. The tar sands are the one thing we have in Canada which will adequately secure the supply of oil to the rest of Canada. The government has taken the position that it will

July 6, 1981
Adjournment Debate
hold them back as long as it has to, that it is control it wants, and security of supply be damned. This is a miscarriage of justice for every man, woman and child in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out two things to the hon. member opposite. First, I do not think the minister misled the hon. member in his reply on July 2. Second, I think to some extent the member himself is misleading the House when he states that the federal government at the present time has no consideration for tar sands development in western Canada.
It has always been a principle behind the National Energy Program to place heavy emphasis upon the development of the tar sands projects in western Canada. The hon. member pointed out rightly that in October, 1980, the minister was prepared to offer the sponsors of those projects $38 per barrel for their oil and in addition a cost of living indexation so that it would be that much more profitable for these companies to develop the tar sands projects.
On July 2 the minister mentioned in the House that in the last several months some statements were made by the people involved in resource development indicating that they were not willing to go ahead with that kind of a joint venture. The minister pointed out that after his meeting with the minister of energy for Alberta on June 29, the project sponsor confirmed that it had dropped all such threats and was encouraged by the significant progress being made in the present negotiations between Ottawa and Alberta. At that time the minister went on to explain to the hon. member opposite that they have had several meetings in the last five to six weeks concerning the energy pricing agreement. Both the federal Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), and his provincial counterpart in Alberta felt that significant progress was being made in reaching an oil pricing agreement.
I want to point out to the hon. member, with respect to the development of the tar sands projects in October, 1980, when the minister offered $38 a barrel with this indexation clause, that it was the Province of Alberta, which under its jurisdiction has the right to grant the licence for the development of the tar sands project, that it was the Province of Alberta which halted it and said that it would have to be part of the whole package in terms of the oil pricing agreement. Thus, the federal government's position has always been clear. We place great emphasis on the need to develop the tar sands projects in western Canada. We feel very strongly that, given the size of those resources, they, in fact, will be very decisive in terms of the ability of Canada to become oil self-sufficient during this decade.
As the minister has pointed out, the tempo of negotiations has been stepped up, with the fourth meeting since May being scheduled within the next few weeks. The minister also wanted to make it known that he feels these are very productive meetings. There is an increasing optimism of a good resolution of these difficult and complex issues.

HAZARDOUS SUBSTANCES-DANGERS OF USE OF MARIJUANA

Mr. Speaker, my question on June 12, 1981 was directed to the Minister of National Research and Welfare (Miss Begin). It reads in part:
In light of the growing advocacy by some members of this House and the press for changes in laws pertaining to possession of marijuana which appear to lessen their severity, will the minister take equally aggressive action to warn and educate the people of this country by every means at her disposal of the long and short term medical dangers and hazardous effects of this drug, and introduce important medical considerations into the implementation of any proposed change?
In the answer given, the minister did not appear to put emphasis on the seriousness of the health dangers and hazardous effects involved with this drug and seemed to give priority to the legal injustices over the medical implications.
Marijuana is a very powerful agent which affects the body in many ways. A copious amount of scientific data has been accumulated in the period from 1975 to 1979. This data has been published in over 2500 scientific papers. Marijuana is unique in that it contains 60 chemicals called cannabinoids, which are not found anywhere else in nature. Of these 60, only five have been studied to any degree of completeness scientifically. The greatest and most intense work has been done on only one of these chemicals, namely, tetrahydro cannabinol, the most mind-altering chemical in marijuana. This drug has a tendency to seep into the fatty tissues of the body, including the brain. It is removed from the body slowly, requiring over 30 days to be completely excreted. Hence, many months are required before the body has totally recovered from the effects of this drug. Moreover, at the time of the LeDain report in the early 1970s, marijuana cigarettes had a THC potency of .5 per cent to 1 per cent. Today marijuana cigarettes contain a 3 per cent to 5 per cent concentration of this drug.
Recent research has shown that five marijuana cigarettes do as much damage as 112 ordinary tobacco cigarettes. Cigarettes containing marijuana have 50 per cent to 100 per cent more cancer producing drugs or chemicals than those of ordinary tobacco cigarettes. One third of the people smoking ordinary tobacco show an incidence of chronic cough and a predisposition to cancer as manifested by atypical cells in their sputum. However, with people smoking marijuana cigarettes, over 61 per cent show an incidence of a chronic cough and 100 per cent show atypical cells in their sputum, which is a step before a pre-cancerous change takes place in the lining of the airways.
Hard evidence is surfacing indicating that marijuana is far more dangerous to the health than suspected. At present, the scientific community is only in the preliminary stages of investigation. Not only does marijuana affect functioning of the body organs and systems but it also affects one's behaviour and performance.
In the field of driving skills, a 1974 British Columbia study has shown convincingly that subjects under the influence of cannabis showed impaired judgment in assessing traffic signals, and their response to rapidly changing environmental
July 6, 1981

situations and their ability to concentrate on driving was impaired.
In the United States post-mortem studies were carried out on drivers involved in traffic fatalities. It was found that 16 per cent of the drivers had used marijuana. This drug was second only to the use of alcohol as a factor in traffic fatalities. Current studies do not give a clear picture of the role played by marijuana in traffic accidents. In the hospitals of this country, it is impossible to assess the concentration of THC in blood by a rapid clinical test. Such a test has not yet been devised and is not available for clinical purposes. The assessment of the concentration of this drug in the blood necessitates a laborious clinical exercise carried out in a forensic laboratory. There is, therefore, a double standard in assessing impaired drivers. For those drivers suspected of being impaired by alcohol, there exists a test which gives a rapid, accurate and a precise indication of the concentration. However, there are no tests for those impaired by cannabis. The use of this drug can be discovered only by its odour, by previous contact with it, by training or by speculated guessing.
There is also considerable evidence suggesting the enhancing effect of cannabis on alcohol. The use of cannabis in combination with alcohol therefore presents another serious hazard in traffic safety. Alcohol is by far the most dangerous, best studied, most understood and publicly accepted intoxicant contributing to traffic accidents. Our knowledge of marijuana and its effects on car accidents is approximately 50 years behind that of alcohol and tobacco. But must we use the trial and error technique to establish its frightful role in traffic accidents and fatalities by allowing its more widespread use, by recommending what appear to be more relaxed marijuana laws, or should we be more cautious in changing any legislation until we really understand the part played by marijuana usage in the mounting traffic tolls?
Epidemiological studies on large segments of the population of users, such as have already been done in relation to alcohol and tobacco, are needed to fill in the gaps in our knowledge. It will take a generation or more of wide-ranging public health observations to provide a clear picture, especially among adolescents who are more susceptible to physical and mental changes due to rapid physiological and psychological development of their bodies.
In an atempt to correct legal injustice, let us not pave the road to greater assault on the body and mind of Canadians by facilitating the use of a powerful intoxicant such as marijuana which is not yet completely understood as far as its medical implications are concerned.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Frith (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Deputy Leader of the Government in the Senate
subtopic: HAZARDOUS SUBSTANCES-DANGERS OF USE OF MARIJUANA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps before
Adjournment Debate
getting into the technical response to the question asked by the hon. member, I want to point out that I think there is some confusion which is being created here by the government's intention to lessen the penalties for possession of small amounts of marijuana. In fact, the rest of my response is predicated on the premise that if and when the government introduces the legislation, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) is prepared to undertake a rather extensive training and educational program for the Canadian public, because I think that the Minister of National Health and Welfare is very much aware of some of the serious side effects that marijuana can, in fact, produce.
This is not to say that when the government introduces this type of legislation we as a government are condoning the use of marijuana; we are simply becoming cognizant of the fact that there are significant numbers of young people in this country who have permanent criminal records because of very small quantities of marijuana being found in their possession. The government intends to continue going after the importers and traffickers of large amounts of marijuana as rigorously as it does under the present legislation.
I want to point out to the hon. member that the minister is aware of studies that have taken place all over the world regarding the side effects of marijuana. As a medical practitioner, I am sure he is aware that the Minister of National Health and Welfare recognizes that the regular use of marijuana, for example, can be as carcinogenic as any other kind of tobacco use; that we are aware that the use of marijuana, for example, can rapidly increase the heart rate of cardiovascular patients; that we are aware that marijuana used by very young people can change the hormonal balance; that there is growing evidence that it has some teratogenic side effects; that its use is not condoned by the government for young people or pregnant women.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare has a responsibility to teach the Canadian public about the health hazards of marijuana. If and when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) introduces the legislation, the Minister of National Health and Welfare will undertake a program of education in collaboration with a number of the provinces and territories which are very anxious to jointly sponsor projects with the federal government. These would explain to the Canadian public the health hazards associated with marijuana.
I want to conclude by saying that it is very important that the public know the federal government does not condone the
